subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 18, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since we adjourned the debate on Tuesday night there has been time for us to learn something of the public reaction to this measure. So far as we have gone I should not think the Minister of Finance has taken much comfort from it. The mildest word I have heard used is "disappointing", and the word "black" has been used almost somewhat freely. The word "vinegar" has also been on people's lips. I shall have something to add to this torrent in my small way.
First of all, I wish to say something about taxation in a general way. It is hard to realize that less than ten years ago, in 1939, when we thought we were paj-ing taxes, we were really paying nothing compared with our present taxes. At that time the per capita tax was $38.76, which for a family of five-let us call it a normal family-would be S194. Of course in those days most of the taxation was in the form of customs and excise which was largely concealed from the ordinary taxpayer so that he was almost unconscious of the fact that it was taxation at all.
In the intervening years the government has invaded our lives deeply. We have to make large payments for interest, and the Minister of Finance takes a large slice of our income for the social services which we have approved. We have made huge additions to our debt because of war, and we have to make
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

large expenditures-perhaps not as large as we may have to make-for defence. A large dollop of our income goes for government-owned enterprises. We are in the railway business, the film business and various other businesses and they nearly all cost money.
I think it is very desirable that the taxpayer should have present in his mind exactly what is happening to him and what it costs to support all these outlets. As I said a moment ago, the federal tax in 1939 was $38.76, but the federal tax is now $198. The total tax from the three taxing jurisdictions is $259 per capita, or roughly $1,300 per family of five. I imagine that there is a feeling in some quarters that that is an average figure which does not mean very much to the average man. It is felt that it is paid by the well-to-do, but there never was a greater mistake than that. It is quite true that people with large incomes are being heavily taxed-and that is having an effect, and the effect is bad, on investment capital- but after all they have paid has been collected it represents only a small fraction of the total. To all intents and purposes the average is spread over the rest of the community. The average family may as well face the fact that that is what it is contributing to the national revenue, that that is what it pays.
I suggest that it is worth looking for a moment to see what it gets. First the average family knows what it gets for its municipal tax. It gets street lighting, education, water and all that kind of thing. It is interesting to note that municipal taxes during that period have not gone up; they have remained almost identically where they were, being roughly still $125 for the family of five. There has been an addition of $875 in that period, almost wholly in the form of dominion taxes. I think it is desirable that the people who carry this burden, the people who are trying to look after themselves, should realize just how much they are paying. After all, SI.300 is not chicken feed. I suggest that if every family knew just what was happening they might take a greater interest in what is going on.
This naturally raises the question of economy. I am not going to say a lot of old things about economy. Not long ago the Minister of Finance said in this house-I sympathize with him-that keeping down expenses was quite a job. He also said that he felt he did more for it-this is a free interpretation of his words-than anyone else in this house. That may be so, but after all he is the only one who really has a chance.
It is hard to abandon wartime spending. Spending is a pleasant thing and, as I say,

it is difficult to get away from it. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply will be glad to have me recall to him what he said in this house in the autumn of 1945 in answer to a question of mine. He said;
I dare say my hon. friend could cut a million dollars from this amount, but a million dollars from the war appropriation bill would not be a very important matter.
It was not a very important matter to him, but in Muskoka-Ontario we think that a million dollars is quite a lot of money. After we have been spending at that rate it is very hard to cut down. I should like to say a word about how the total number in the civil service has grown. I recognize that there are reasons for great growth, but the figures are interesting. In 1939 there were 46,000 civil servants; in 1944 the number had grown to 113,000, and in 1946 to 137,000. The full figure, including those in government corporations, at the peak was 173,000, from which there has been a substantial recession.
It is hard to know whether the post-war economy effort has slackened at all when there are still over 150,000 people in government employ. I suggest that there is always a great deal that could be done if only the Minister of Finance could harden his heart enough. I suggest to him, with every desire to be helpful, and I am sure he knows that that is always my wish, that there is only one way to economize, and that is to give people less money to spend.
It seems to me that if the minister gets involved in arguments with departmental heads about the reasonableness of what they would like to have, he is lost before he begins. If the minister could somehow or other put himself in a frame of mind when he is going over these items of having a deficit, of actually believing that the money is not there; if he could only say to department A or department B, "That is all you can get," I think he would be amazed to see how somehow or other they would get along with the money he would give them.
I heard of a manufacturer who had a pleasant and simple theory that there were two kinds of employees in a business, those who produced and those who did not produce. Among those who did not produce he included the clerical staff. He came into the managership of a new company where he found a clerical staff of about forty. He fired the lot of them. After that he began to take them back gradually one by one, but he took them back only as it was established to his satisfaction that they were really needed. I am not suggesting any such heroic measure to the Minister of Finance, but I am suggesting that there

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
is only one way of getting economy; that is, he should not argue with people over what they would like to spend; he should tell the departments what he is going to allow them. After all, the trouble about the minister is that he can come along and put his hands in our pockets. If he were not able to do that I think he would find that people would manage to get along with less.
There is another kind of expenditure that is made, which while not very large in itself, is bad because it creates a most unfortunate impression on the public mind. I refer to the expenditures made for various kinds of commissions. Take for example, the price spreads committee. It is going to cost the country a lot of money. The Minister of Trade and Commerce will say that it is just chicken feed because he does not think a million dollars is any money at all, but when the ordinary taxpayer finds out how much it is costing for lawyers, for accountants, for stenographers and all the various incidentals, he will think it is quite a lot of money.
When we set up bodies of this kind I think it is proper to ask just what they are going to do. It is not fair to take this price spreads committee because it has been such a fiasco. It was beaten before it started. I feel sorry for my friend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who has had to preside over it, because, as I say, from the start he was beaten. If he did not find that prices were extravagantly swollen, he was going to fail; on the other hand, if he found that they were swollen, he would be criticizing government departments, the department of investigation and the department of control, for not keeping them down.
As I say, that kind of commission is undesirable. Compared to other large expenditures it will not be much, but I think it creates an impression in the public mind that we are careless with their money. I do not think parliament should be asked to lend itself to that kind of thing.
I come now to the minister's surplus. The other night he said it was of a nature to gladden the heart of a finance minister. But I do not think it should have gladdened his heart, and I am not sure it did, because in the latter part of his speech he spoke more realistically about it. It rather should have saddened his heart, for this reason:	the surplus was due, first, to the unfortunate rise in prices, which jumped the taxes; second, to the tremendous spate of buying from the United States, which also greatly increased taxes, and third, to bad estimating.
I come now to the minister's taxation proposals. I have referred already to the widespread disappointment. Of course the trouble is that people want to spend their own money. They think they know how to do that better than governments, and they would like to have as much of their own money to spend as possible.
I said that I approved of budgeting for a surplus, and so I do; but the question is how much of a surplus? On that I would like to say a word further.
The reason I believe in budgeting for a surplus is this. From time to time there are bound to be periods of lesser activity during which, when you consider the obligations which the state has now assumed, we shall have to budget for deficits. Therefore if in a time of large income we .do nothing to pay off debt, then the debt is going to go up and up and up, and in the end confidence will be destroyed. Nevertheless it is pertinent and proper to discuss how much the surplus should be. The minister was cagey in discussing this; he played with his cards very close to his chest. The one universal comment made when the minister was through was: Well, no election this year. The reason is obvious. The reason was that the minister did not, like little Jack Horner, put in his thumb and pull out a plum. He was very chary about distributing anything that even looked like a plum, and that gave rise to the thought that the plums were being kept until later. That might be a suspicion of unworthy minds; nevertheless it was widely entertained, and it was what everybody had in mind when they said: No election this year. This may be said: if the hard-pressed taxpayer is being denied relief this year in order that at some later time, with an election pending, little Jack Horner may put in his thumb and pull out a plum, that is wrong, and the taxpayer should resent it, and it should be chanved before this budget passes the house.
Let me look for a moment at the figures. The minister is budgeting in the coming year for a surplus of 1489 million. Last year he budgeted for $190 million, and he explained that that would be reduced by $110 million if the three provinces, that had not come to agreement with the federal government, came in. Let me repeat those figures. Last year he budgeted for $190 million, and tax relief of $160 million. This year he is budgeting for a surplus of $489 million; and he is giving tax relief nominally of $60,000,000, but really it is only $40,000,000 because $20,000,000 of that is in the amusement tax, and that involves merely a change in the burden, so it is really only $40,000,000.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

Let us take this $489 million. Last year the minister's actual surplus was $460 million move than the estimate. He budgeted for $190 million and his actual surplus was $650 million. I am not suggesting that there is going to be any such excess this year. I do not think there will be. Nevertheless I feel confident that the budgeting is done very cautiously. Nobody wants to be caught out in overestimating. I think it is resonable to assume that $489 million might become $500 million or $600 million or more, but I am not going to press the argument. I am going to assume that it is practically, say, $500 million. If the debt reduction were the only thing we had to think about, no one would be more pleased than I to see $500 million used in paying off debt. But that is not the only thing we have to think about. There is the fact in the first place, that living costs have gone up considerably, and it is important to relieve the hard-pressed low-income taxpayers. Secondly, we still need to provide incentive, because we still have a situation in which the government in one way or another has been providing a terrific incentive to industry, and one day that will have to be done by ourselves. Therefore I say it is important to have the incentive. There is a third reason which it is proper to take into consideration, and it is this. We are in danger of being faced with a new tide of wage demands, and if anything can be done to relieve the cost of living in the lower income brackets I think it should be done, and done without delay.
I would like to read a word or two from a broadcast in England the other day by the Right Hon. Oliver Stanley, because i't is relevant to the problem we are discussing now. Speaking of the British budget on April 7 last he said:
We don't quarrel with the need for a substantial surplus, but we do differ from the chancellor as to the way he has got to get it
He had a choice: he could get it by imposing heavy expenditure and still heavier taxation, or he could get it by a substantial reduction in expenditure, with a lower rate of taxes.
Unfortunately he chose the first, and by doing so he stopped himself offering any large tax reductions to encourage incentive and increase production-the other and the better way of fighting inflation.
One further quotation from Mr. Stanley- and this has particular relevance to this budget:
Make no mistake: however necessary such a budget may be in these dangerous times, it does not by itself get us anywhere. The real relief will only come with greater production, and that will only come with greater freedom and greater incentive. Fewer controls and lower taxes: that is what we want to see.

In the light of that I venture to suggest to the Minister of Finance that there are certain things he could do and do now. I suggest that there should be a contribution to the cost of living by an increase in the exemptions for people in the low income brackets. Just in case anyone wishes to know if I have a figure in mind, I say no; but I have had an inquiry made and I think I am in a position to reach the conclusion that a substantial measure of relief could be given to those in the low income brackets at a cost to the treasury of not more than 25 per cent of this figure of $500 million, which I have taken as the likely surplus.
There is one other thing I want to suggest, and I think it is of very great importance. I am sure everyone will agree, even those who do not share the view that private enterprise is the solution to our economic problems, that the lifeblood of private enterprise is that new and small businesses should constantly be coming into the picture and be encouraged to become bigger. Those of us who believe in freedom, and are just as strong as anyone else in disliking monopoly, believe that that is the way to do it. Therefore I suggest that the minister might take into consideration the giving of some relief to small enterprises-and I mean small enterprises of any kind. Someone asked me if that would include a farmer, and I said yes- anyone who incorporates his business and therefore comes within the four corners of the corporation tax act. I suggest to the minister, and again I am not going to give a figure, that it might be desirable, in cases where income is reinvested in the business, where there is no question of anyone taking it out, but where income is really invested and becomes the means of further employment and further production, there should be an amount at the bottom which is free of tax, and an amount above that where the tax might be five per cent, another amount where it might be ten per cent, and another where it might be fifteen per cent, the full tax to become payable at a comparatively modest amount. I repeat that I think such a measure would be of great benefit; and while I am not attempting to estimate its cost, I would think its cost at the present time would be very little indeed.
So far we have been considering what you might call the dividing up of the cake that we have. We have a certain amount. How are we to divide it up? I want to turn to a larger area-far more important in one way, because our whole welfare is bound up in government policy here. After all, whether we like it or not, government is in our affairs, government

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
is influencing us at every turn, and it becomes of tremendous importance whether they make right decisions or wrong ones-because they are making decisions, and big decisions, all the time.
Having said this, I turn to the question of trade. There is no need to waste the time of the house one second to say how vital trade is to all of us. On December 9 the Prime Min-itser began a debate on the Geneva trade agreements. By an unhappy chance, Mr. Speaker, these agreements were announced almost on the day, perhaps on the very day, that we also had announced the spate of embargoes, permits, quotas and all these other things which the Minister of Finance denounced the other day, quite sincerely I am sure, but which unfortunately have been forced upon us. In other words, the government found itself in the position of opening the door to trade with one hand and banging it shut with the other.
It would appear as if in this case the Prime Minister's instinct for timing had failed. The other da}' the Prime Minister was kind enough to give some advice-he gave it in a kindly way, as the Minister of Labour would say-to my leader. I am now going to read what the Prime Minister was kind enough to say the other day. He said, as reported at page 3939 of Hansard:
I give my hon. friend a word of counsel. It is always wise to try to anticipate all possibilities before they arise. In so doing you do not find yourself unnecessarily embarrassed when the important moment comes.
I am inclined to think that the Prime Minister would regard what happened last autumn as an exception, perhaps one of the very few exceptions, to his successful following of his own advice. I will say to the Prime Minister that if he was embarrassed when he made that speech on the Geneva agreements, I did not see any sign of it. I regret that he made a first-class political speech, not the kind of speech I hoped he would make. I hoped he might have taken the trade agreements out of politics, but he did not; he put them right in.
In opening the debate the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 100 of Hansard:
I should like to say that it is a source of particular satisfaction to me that the present agreement should be so completely in line with what has been the policy of the Liberal party in Canada from the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier down to the present time,-
I was sorry to note that apparently Alexander Mackenzie and Edward Blake no longer enter into the picture. I hope that does not mean that Sir Wilfrid Laurier himself will
ever be forgotten. At any rate that is what the Prime Minister said. He went on to add:
-and that it should be my privilege to present it to our parliament. The Liberal party has always been in the van in the struggle for greater freedom of trade.
Further on he said:
The party has always acted on the belief that prosperity is inevitably associated with extensive and general international commerce.
It is interesting, in the light of that, to look at the Liberal budget of 1930, which, I think I am correct in saying, gave the tariff its biggest single hoist since 1878; and of course we all remember the steel pipe duties in the autumn of 1945, when unfortunately the Prime Minister himself was away. So far as we can judge there was a bit of mutiny across the gangway at that time. At any rate we know this, that the increases in the duties were abandoned. Whether it was by reason of the master's voice from Winnipeg is really not a question we need pursue further.
These jarring notes of 1930 and 1945 are mild compared with what has been done since. We all remember the exchange conservation bill. A moment ago I referred to the spate of exclusions, quotas, permits and all these special powers given to the minister, to whom I must not refer in any way that he will not like.
The Prime Minister did not take part in the debate on the exclusion and conservation bill. I imagine the Prime Minister was embarrassed-at any rate too much embarrassed to take part in that debate. I imagine he realized the truth of the words of the negro gentleman who said: "Massa, dem two things don't paralyse."
I now want to come to the remedial measures, which were quite highly advertised last autumn. They do not seem to be working very well. The imports in January and February of this year stood at $287 million, which I understand is a record. There is an interesting circumstance there. Capital goods are coming in freely. Apparently the only people who have actually suffered are housewives, and people who, like the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), like lettuce and other innocent things of that kind. They have suffered, but capital goods are coming in. No doubt the minister, as I shall point out later, committed himself to an extravagant and unwise policy of special depreciation.
According to the minister, last autumn we were going to correct our difficulties largely by increasing our export of manufactured goods to the United States. I should like

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
Hoffman, European administrator, signed with other members of the national advisory council, a report sent to congress that the United States will require countries getting ERP aid to work out devaluation with the 46-nation world monetary fund.
I was interested to find in the most recent Economist that even the International Monetary Fund apparently is seriously considering the situation, that it has its eyes and its mind by no means closed.
I have been talking about what I regard as a distortion of our economy in our external economic relations. I now wish to talk briefly about what I regard as a distortion at home. Before the end of the war, in the spring of 1945, the government issued a white paper designed to deal with conditions after the war, when it was expected there would be some unemployment; and at the time I think the precaution was reasonable. If the unemployment had in fact come I should think the measures proposed would have had much to commend them. But what I complain about, and what I think has been little short of a tragedy, is that we continued to use those measures long after it was perfectly clear that we should have done exactly the opposite. Signs of the boom really appeared in 1946, and the methods outlined in 1945 should have been altered then, and altered quickly. Instead, the government continued to use them and even accelerated them. What we needed was a sedative; what we got was a strong tonic. What do I mean by that? I mean that the government did two things. It powerfully stimulated plant expansion by what I think were extravagant inducements in the way of depreciation, and it also continued to pursue an easy money policy, which was the other method of encouragement.
Now I want to say a word about this double depreciation. Let us understand exactly what it means. It means that companies are offered special inducements to go ahead and expand their plants as rapidly as possible. In this case they were allowed to deduct especially large amounts of money when that money was reinvested in the business, and so escape taxation on it. The plant expansion under way through the use of this double depreciation is estimated in a government report to cost $1,400 million. That is a terrific amount to impose on the economy of our country. According to this report, a survey of some four thousand companies, 2,241 of them in operation in 1939 and 1,971 coming into operation since, shows that these companies, when alterations are completed, will have a manufacturing capacity of -SS * 5 billion, as against $1-8 billion in 1939. In other words the excess

over 1939 is 377 per cent. The comparable figure in the United States is 50 per cent. That is, proportionately we have gone seven and a half times as fast as the United States.
I mentioned the other evening that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said: "Well, what's the matter with that?"-or words to that effect. The answer is this. If we can find markets for all these things; if we can sell all these goods and our producers of natural products can also sell all their goods, so that we will have the home market and the foreign market, that will be fine. But whether or not that is likely to happen remains to be seen. The other evening I used a simple illustration. I hope I am wrong-this is one time I would like to be wrong and see the minister right; but I used the example of a farmer straining himself and using all his resources to build a huge barn, which incidentally may turn out to be more than he needs, and at the same time neglecting to provide his family with the necessities of life.
The immediate result of this development is that an inordinate amount of our resources is turned toward this plant expansion, which means far less for the production of consumer goods, which in turn means this has been a most potent influence in the rising prices of consumer goods. AVe have been providing the money but we have not been providing the goods; and even those of us who do not profess to be economists know that this is a simple reason for high prices.
I sometimes fear that Canadian businessmen are taking this matter much too lightly. I think they are being led astray by what has been going on abroad. I have heard Canadian businessmen say, "Markets are illimitable; we we can sell anything we make". But this buying spree abroad is not going on for ever. As European nations become able to look after themselves there will be less need to buy from us. In the meantime I say again that at the very time our relations with the United States are so difficult, and when we really have not improved our position at all in spite of our restrictions, we are denying our manufacturers the advantage they had before July 1946 in selling in the United States. AVe have taken away a ten per cent advantage they formerly enjoyed.
When I refer to exchange, however, to me a convincing argument and one that outweighs all others is the appeal to realism. AVhen you find things happening between people who are trading with each other freely, that comes as close to realism as you can get. To me it is not real for us here in Canada to sit in an ivory tower saying our dollar is worth one

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
hundred American cents when actually it is being traded in the United States at between 92 and 93 cents. We too much resemble King Canute.
In passing, and coming back to this question of the export of manufactured goods, I want to say that if we can build these hundreds and in fact thousands of factories, and if they can all export their goods, it will be splendid; but we must remember that if we try to export to the point where we are not able to buy enough to provide our producers with their natural markets, the first people to feel the effects will be the manufacturers, because the home market after all is their best market.
I want to say a word about the investment aspect. How did we provide all this money in 1947? It was not by savings. Personal savings amounted to only S768 million in 1947 as against SI,676 million in 1944. The gap was filled largely by the realization of $750 million of our American exchange; in other words we were living off our fat. The amount was realized and paid to the banks, and became available; indirectly it appeared in effect in the large increase in bank loans. The second thing was the government surplus of last year.
I am going to say a word about savings, though one is almost self-conscious in talking about savings these days. Many people think that is a silly old-fashioned thing only talked about by people who are still living in the nineteenth century. My own belief is that there is great danger in the view which is so widely held that wealth consists in pieces of paper. If only we could think of it in terms of goods I believe we would be much more sensible. If we would also remember that at the present time we are living largely on savings, as I say both government realizations and the savings of private individuals who are spending more than they are saving, as a whole, we would appreciate how important it is. I wish I could make people believe that I think common sense in government one day will prove to be the same common sense that has to apply to individuals; that governments cannot by any legerdemain produce money over the long period, any more than individuals can. If we believe the government can do that, and if we go on believing that there is some secret way by which money can be created, then I say we are just piling up difficulties which one day will recoil upon our own heads. In the long run we have to provide personal savings for investment, just as we have done in the past.
I have dealt with foreign trade, Mr. Speaker, and with what I regard as the distortion of our economy at home. I have said something about the post-war inflation and the post-war boom. I have spoken about the artificial stimulus to our economy, and I want to say one thing more. I want to say a word about the manipulation of the bond market. Prices in the bond market are no longer made, as they always have been made in the past, by hundreds or thousands of individuals buying and selling. They are made by a few men sitting in a room here in Ottawa. How is that done? It is done by the support given the bond market through the Bank of Canada. The evils of this sort of thing have become apparent within the last few months. In January last, on account of an altered attitude on the part of the bank, the price of bonds fell from 104J to lOlf. Later, I think about the beginning of February, the price fell again from 101J to 100L This, of course, was without warning to the business community; it had to be. One can well imagine the embarrassment of executors, trustees and others who had been holding these bonds and since have had to sell them. Incidentally, if the government itself has suffered any loss in its transactions through its various boards, I would be interested to know where it gets the authority for the appropriation to pay such losses. That is another matter, however, which we can take up later.
The technique of course is the use of government funds through certain bodies which have been created. There is the unemployment insurance fund, and there is a fund called the security investment fund, in which the financial community has been much interested for a long time. It was a rather mysterious fund until very recently, but I noticed the other night, if I remember correctly, that the Minister of Finance spoke about it frankly. I may be partly responsible for that, because recently I asked a question about it. I asked what the authority for this fund was, and I was referred to two statutes. Well, when you are refereed to two statutes, even a man who knows as little law as I do, knows that the authority is pretty hard to find. You have to spell it out. It is not clear and distinct and inescapable. When I got those two statutes I took counsel from someone who is a real lawyer-not just a reformed lawyer like myself-and asked him what he thought about those two statutes. He told me you could not spell any authority out of them at all. So I am leaving that question. We can find out all about it later. Meantime in six months that fund has spent $300 million of your money and mine in buying bonds in the market, and the fund has in fact now about $600 million.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

I say, in that connection as in others, that we shall one day return to reality. We shall one day decide to question the judgment of two or three people sitting in an office; for however able they may be, however conscientious or however high-minded, they have not omniscience or supreme wisdom. Against them is the judgment of hundreds of thousands of quiet people who just buy and sell from day to day, matching their judgment against each other. They are going to find that that is the way prices are made, not by this superhuman wisdom.
It is interesting to note what has been going on in England, where there is a socialist government. Of course they have there this new revelation. At any rate Doctor Dalton believed it, and I should like to bring to the attention of the house briefly what happened in England, what the London Economist has described as an unwholesome and unpleasant precedent.
Doctor Dalton was a former chancellor of the exchequer. He undertook to support a certain security there, with disastrous results. The London Economist says this:
A corner has been lifted this week (May 8) of the thick curtain which has shrouded last year's official activities in the gilt-edge market. In the past, the technique of governmental accounting has generally sufficed ... to hide most departmental activities from the public gaze, but operations so large as Doctor Dalton's were bound to peep out through the screen sooner or later.
I commend that to the Minister of Finance. I think some of his operations are beginning to peep out, too. The London Economist continues:
In the pre-budget phase last autumn "Daltons"-
The securities, not as a compliment, were called by Dalton's name.
-rose by some ten points, only to collapse after their sponsor disappeared from the scene.
It will be noted that these securities were called "Daltons." I hope the Minister of Finance will never be memorialized in the same way. However, their sponsor disappeared from the scene. I hope this will be taken as a warning by those who may have any disposition to imitate the good Doctor Dalton. He undertook to impose his will on the bond market, just as our financial authorities are doing today. In the end what he succeeded in doing was to destroy confidence in the particular security he was supporting, so that the security fell disastrously in value.
In a world, Mr. Speaker, which is racked with conflict between those who believe in

freedom and those who, whether they realize it or not, believe in control, I think even at the risk of iteration it is necessary to express what we at least feel in the matter. I do this especially as I shall be followed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and I shall be surprised if he does not use words which we have heard before-the words "exploiting" and "law of the jungle." I am Dot suggesting that what I am going to say now is ill directed against the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, because I sometimes have hopes for the hon. member -just as hon. members opposite have had hopes of him in the past. But I do think these things should be said.
First of all, those of us who have the belief that it is not through an extension of public ownership that social security and prosperity will come should not flatter ourselves that it is by any means a belief which is held universally. There are many people who think they have it but who by their actions occasionally show that they have not got it. For instance I cannot quite believe that the thirty-eight per cent of the people who, according to a Gallup poll in February, said they wished to work for the government, would regard themselves as socialists. Nevertheless to me it is disturbing to find that this poll, taken in February, showed that thirty-eight per cent of those who were questioned said they would rather work for the government than for private business.
What does that mean? Obviously it does not mean that I am criticizing any civil servants. We have some of the finest people in the civil service. But I believe an intelligent civil servant would be the first to say that this is a terribly dangerous situation to have abroad. So far as I have been able to discover, in all governments, municipal, provincial and federal, we have about six per cent of the people gainfully employed-that is not six per cent of the whole population, but of people in employment. Here we have about thirty-eight per cent of the people saying they would rather work for the government. What does that mean? I suggest it indicates a deep and disturbing psychological condition. It means that people have taken up the instinct for security, that they want freedom from responsibility, that they want work-yes, work, honest work, decent work, but a limited amount of it, so that they may have plenty of leisure. It is an abandonment of the spirit of adventure, of the driving energy and initiative which, as most of us think, have brought us where we are. I say that unless we stem

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
the tide we have no hope of going steadily forward to improve our present economic position.
What do I mean by that? Well, I can illustrate it best by telling of a little conversation I had the other day with a man in my riding-or what I hope is going to be my riding, because it was in Parry Sound. This man is a general merchant, a man of great energy, one of the people who make democracy tick in that area. He said to me, "I work fifteen hours a day. But if the government took over my business and made me the manager of it, I would not work fifteen hours a day. I would work eight hours a day five days a week, and I would ask for two or three assistants". What am I saying? Well, I am not saying, of course, that people should be asked to work fifteen hours a day; of course not. But I am saying that the reason why free enterprise is alble to achieve what it does is that a considerable number of people are putting into their work every last ounce of energy they have. If it takes fifteen hours, they will put it in.
I suggest there is all the difference in the world between honest and conscientious performance on the one hand, and on the other the performance of a man with drive and energy who is not content unless he does his absolute best. I do not think there would be any doubt in this matter if people would only think clearly. I suggest that is part of our trouble, part of the difference between us and the people to our left-although I must say sometimes I think there is not very much difference. In fact I would quote something said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and I am pleased to quote it. I think I like quot-ting it better than he likes hearing it. He said one day-and I like to remind him of it -"I am not opposed to private enterprise, but if they take the profits, they must take the risks". I said to him, and I say again: I do not change a word of that. But there is all the difference in the world between that and some of the other things the hon. member says.
To come back to clear thinking-

The digression that I made from clear thinking was a small one; I was just quoting the hon. member.
When reading the life of Mr. Justice Brandeis of the United States Supreme Court I ran across a quotation I should like to give to the house. Mr. Justice Brandeis was a lawyer; he was a queer lawyer because he 5849-270
actually made money. He was a great public servant. No one ever doubted that. He was a liberal-a human liberal, not a political liberal. Mr. Justice Brandeis served the state and the man on the street as very few people have. He said something which I think we might all remember. He said:
Justice is truth in action, and if we want justice we must first find out what is the truth.
I think in plain words that means that unless we have intellectual honesty the thing will not work.
I want now to refer to what I think are some of the misconceptions which are plaguing us at the present time and which again I feel would disappear if we had clear thinking.
First of all there is the misconception of what I call the split personality, that we can be economically bound and politically free. I do feel that should be abandoned once and for all. What does the phrase "democratic socialism" mean? If it is not the equivalent to "free controls", then I do not know what it is. When we look at Italy, Germany and Russia, we realize that we should not be deceived by words. We should note what has happened there. Let us not be deceived by the words "nazism", "fascism", "communism"; it is all state socialism. That is in fact what they are.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the Scandinavian countries?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You can bring them up if you like. As I understand it, they are not socialist in the sense that the countries to which these other names are given are. I am sure that there cannot be any over-all economic control without political control. They are finding that out even in England. As far as labour is concerned, in view of the blight of the three despotisms in Europe I never can understand why labour has any doubt. A United States professor puts it in these words when he says:
There is no place for collective bargaining or the right to strike, or for effective occupational organization in the socialist state, and every intelligent socialist, whatever his public utterances, knows as much.
There is the second misconception that those who believe in freedom, that those who do not want the state to be Father Christmas are lacking in social conscience. It even seems sometimes that to be socially-minded you must refuse to think clearly; you must use catch phrases, and most of all you must try to create the impression that what one man
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

has is taken from another. If a man happens to have more than another man, it is assumed that he has taken it from him.
Mr. MaeINNIS: It usually is so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to refer to what I regard as the classic example, the case of Edison. Edison became rich, but I suggest that Edison created hundreds or thousands of times as much wealth for others as he did for himself. Furthermore, in a greater or lesser degree that is true of every successful enterprise. Churchill put it very well when he said that the people we ought to complain about are not the people who succeed but the people who fail.
The third misconception that is sedulously put forth-I wish every sensible and intelligent man could reach an agreement on this- is that somehow or other profit is wrong and ignoble. I should like to read a quotation from a man who at the present time is a labour peer. He is a well-known leftist in England; in fact some people would call him a socialist. A. D. Lindsay is a well-known writer on politics and economics. I have forgotten his title; it is hard to trace them when they become lords. He said;
If we consider profit in itself it does not seem clear why a man working for an assured salary is doing right, while a man working for an uncertain profit is doing wrong. As long as there is an element of uncertainty in the supplying of demand, there must be a profit.
As I have said, in some of his moods the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar appears to agree with that.
Another thing I should like to say is that profit comes away down on the list. First of all there are wages, then there are taxes, then there is upkeep of your plant, then there is depreciation. If there is anything else, then there is profit. Profit can be obtained only when everyone else is paid. Even at that stage the tax collector, the genial Minister of Finance, comes along and has his crack at it. If there are profits they are well taxed.
I think we should remember that the financial statement of a business is a profit and loss account. There is nobody to hold your hand; nobody to weep a tear for you, if there are losses. You just go broke; that is all there is to it.
I should like to remind hon. gentlemen that even the socialist government in England, which has done so much to try to alter all this, has had to go back to providing an incentive. Let me read from a white paper which says:
We must remove the idea of spinning out production in order to avoid unemployment, or of restricting output in order to safeguard earnings.

It may be that in the back of their minds was the thought that it was capitalist America which had come to the rescue of good old England and all the other countries concerned.
There is one last thing on this point that I want to say, and you will be glad, sir, it is the last. An attempt is made in this country from time to time to stir up class feelings, the sort of thing which has bedevilled some of the European countries. Even England, which we all admire and love so much, has suffered from social disabilities. Was it not Disraeli who said that there were two races in England? It was a fact not so long ago that the slum boy of thirteen years was five inches shorter than the boy who attended public school. That is on the way to being wiped out, and it should be. In England an end is coming to these social disabilities and inhibitions. But here we have not had that. How could it be so in a country where 99-9 per cent of us go to school together? We all speak the same way. There is no barrier to ability.
Mr. MaeINNIS; How many go to univeristy together?
Mr. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario); Every man who has ability.
Mr. MaeINNIS: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 know something about that. I will tell the world that any able man who wants to do it can get to university.
This brings me to opportunity. We in this party nail opportunity to the mast. We seek to help people to help themselves and among other things to provide their own security on a contributory basis.
Mr. Speaker, nature and our forebears provided us with a goodly heritage. By our own efforts and sacrifices we have added to it. Our progress to this present has depended on the free play of the human spirit in all departments of life including the economic. Some point to the war as a time when we made progress through control. It is true that during the war we needed controls in order to concentrate our efforts, but to the discerning eye it was clear that the achievements during the war depended on the same qualities of energy and initiative which capitalism had displayed in peace time.
The great bulk of the people in this country believe that these same qualities are needed to carry us on from here.
People are sensible. They know we cannot get rid of all controls tomorrow, perhaps ever, but they want to have them reduced as much as possible. However, governments will have

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
to play a part beyond what they used to do, and electors should bear this in mind when they are considering the worth of governments which they elect, and in considering the present budget they will have to ask whether it is what it is because the government wishes to keep the plums for some future time.
This budget I think may fairly be described as a doctrinaire budget, a budget that has taken very little consideration of the man on the street. Take, for instance, the small relief in the sales tax. It is ironical to think of the sales tax being taken off when many people have still to pay an extra twenty-five per cent excise tax on their goods. In considering this budget the ordinary citizen may very well consider what happens-and it is bound to happen, human nature being what it is-when governments stay in power year after year after year. Even the best of them develop a kind of bland arrogance. They come to think, not necessarily that they are perfect, but at least that they are indispensable. They come to have what a famous statesman called in other circumstances a tranquil consciousness of effortless superiority, and this gives them the feeling that they can manage other people's affairs much better than the people can manage them themselves. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is.very unlikely that the government in that frame of mind will be able to divest themselves of these powers as fast as they should. They will try to do so but they will find it difficult. It is in any event for the electors to judge whether the government have that openness of mind and that sensitiveness to public opinion which the solution of these problems demands. The widespread criticism of the budget makes me feel that the public at the present time may be exercising their judgment and that no matter how many election plums may be saved up by the government to offer them at election time, they may weigh this government in the balance and find them wanting.
I move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the government does not possess the confidence of the country."

Mr. Speaker, I think we have had a delightful dissertation from the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) which we have all enjoyed. I do not propose to follow his example and to take up the time which I wish to devote to the budget by replying to 5849-270*
some of his remarks or to returning in kind some of the criticisms that one could make of the party to which he belongs. But I am going to say this to him with regard to the hope that he expressed regarding myself, that there is an old proverb which says that "hope deferred maketh the heart sick." I would remind him also that the definition of "fascism" and "nazism" is this: It is capitalism in an advanced state of decay. My hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party should take that very much to heart, because I have noticed that there is considerable decay in the party to my left-to my right, I mean.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were right the first lime.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We sometimes think of the party to the left as somewhat of a conservative party too.
May I also say this to my hon. friend, that the objection is not to profit in the sense that he defined it this afternoon but rather to profit when it becomes the motive of production and replaces human need as the motive for producing the goods that humanity requires.
I think we can all agree that the budget is a disappointing document, though the minister delivered his speech well. It gives little or no relief to the people who need it most. That, I think, is the main criticism which can be made of the budget which was brought down on Tuesday evening.
It is sound policy to budget for a surplus in time of prosperity, but that does not excuse the government from its obligation to assist those whom its policies of removing beneficial controls and subsidies have seriously affected. The gap between prices and income has become wider as the months have passed, and it is obvious that the fifty per cent or so of our population who do not earn enough money to pay income tax have had to reduce their already meagre expenditures on food and clothing and, where possible, on housing also. The reductions in food expenditure which are taking place will in time seriously affect both the health and the morale of those who are compelled to economize in that manner.
I wish to draw the attention of the house to the report of the Family Service Bureau at Hamilton, Ontario, which points out that most families had to spend from 24 to 39 per cent of their income, or amounts ranging from $24 to $45 a month, for food in 1939, and they must now spend from 40 to 80 per cent of their income, or from $50 to more than $100 a month, for the same standard of food in quality and quantity.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In his budget speech last year, at page 2558 of Hansard, the present minister justified his retention of the excess profits tax to the end of 1947, and he justified it by stating that profits had not yet returned to normal levels, and that if they had we should repeal the tax forthwith. He then said:
Profits before tax still are running at abnormally high levels.
But they were running at more abnormally high levels than the minister was estimating at that time. His estimate last year of corporate profits and other investment income was $42,000,000 less than the more accurate estimate he gave in the appendix to the budget speech this year. Even so, the preliminary 1947 figures show that corporate profits before taxes for 1947 were some $400 million, or 28-1 per cent higher than in 1946, and that net profits after taxes were 35-4 per cent higher.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

Lest these figures should be disputed, I wish to put on the record again table 7, in the appendix to the 1948 budget, page 4112 of Hansard, which gives us the corporation profits from 1939 to 1947. It is a very short table and I should like to have the permission of the house to put it on Hansard.
