This criticism I have made justifies the criticisms we made last year of the removal of the excess profits tax which, had it been retained, would have had an effect on the ability of the government either to decrease taxation on those least able to bear it, or, on the other hand, to have embarked upon a more substantial health and social security program for the Canadian people, while at the same time securing quite a substantial budgetary surplus, though perhaps not as high as the estimate at the moment.
The minister recognizes the dangers inherent in the high level of capital expenditure on new construction. He blames it, together with the high level of domestic consumption and exports, for the undue strain on our economy, and I wish to say something about this matter particularly.
Many years ago, the Liberal party, like the C.C.F., proposed the control of investments, and the minister's speech indicated that capital construction, that is, investment in plant, equipment, inventories and such housing as was undertaken, absorbed twenty-one per cent of the gross national product during 1947 as against fifteen per cent in 1946, six per cent in 1944 and, going back a few years, sixteen per cent in 1939. It may be remarked, I think that fluctuations in capital construction are mainly responsible for the ups and downs of the business cycle and for the consequent booms and depressions.
I recognize that many expenditures for new plant, equipment, machinery and so on had been deferred during ten long years of depression and six years of war. Consequently there is now a rush by everyone to replace worn-out machines, to buy equipment, and so on, all at once. What is happening is that construction, which should ordinarily spread over a period of sixteen years, is being squeezed into a very few short years. Everyone is building factories, new theatres, new bowling alleys, new breweries and replacing worn-out machines all at once. The danger is, as the minister saw himself, and indicated in his budget speech, that by and by we shall reach the saturation point, and when we do so, then activity will drop sharply and the effects of such a drop will be extremely widespread throughout the whole of the Canadian economy.
The minister recognizes this danger, and that is evident in his statement that this government has, of course, been deliberately restricting its own expenditures on construction and

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
equipment during the last few years because of its desire to keep excessive national expenditure within bounds, and to divert wherever possible the construction of useful projects until the time when private expenditures will be lower and additional government work will help to maintain employment and income.
The theory is that the government should allow private construction to take its own course, the government being ready to fill the gap left by private enterprise when that gap occurs. I will say this to the minister. In my opinion, this is a decided improvement over the old laissez-faire attitude, but it is still a questionable procedure in terms of actual effectiveness.
The C.C.F. believes that the government should exercise some control not only over government investment but over private investment as well. May I remind the minister that a few years ago that was also the policy advocated by the Liberal party. The effect which government construction spending can have is, I believe, too small in the ordinary course of events to save the country from a major unemployment crisis which will follow unusually high capital construction in this period in which we are living. In our opinion, and we would urge it upon the government, the government should take positive steps, so that private investment spending in some respects should be deferred to later periods and priority given to such desirable and necessary projects as low-rental housing which the house has been discussing for several days this week, during which I hope the government felt rather uncomfortable about the results achieved so far. Such a policy would not only relieve the desperate housing shortage but have long-range effects in relieving the inflationary pressures which are responsible for steadily climbing prices.
What I mean is this. The public control of investment should not only be quantitative, which is to a minor extent what is happening now, but be qualitative as well. Construction contracts for hotels and clubs in Canada last year totalled $14,750,000, but for apartments in which people were going to live they amounted to only $12,070,000.
This, of course, is only one of a number of examples that could be cited. Then, too, we believe the government should exercise some influence on the location of desirable industries. The distressed areas of England and Wales and Scotland, for example, are becoming the sites of great, new and important industries. In the same way some construction expenditure could be diverted to the distressed areas of Canada; and we have those distressed
areas. As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) so frequently reminds the house, we have them in the maritime provinces; and to my mind this is what might be called a socially desirable project of the very first order.
In the same circumstances what would a C.C.F. government do? It would establish a national investment board which would exercise control over investments, so that they could be spread over a number of years and diverted into channels where they would be most effective, and establish priority for the most important types of construction, as, for example, housing. Because we believe this, I want to move an amendment to the amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), in these words:
That the said amendment be amended by inserting after the word' "government" and before the word "does" in the second line of the amendment, the following words:
". . . has failed to relieve the excessive burden of taxation on the low-income groups of the Canadian people:
(a)	By failing to increase the amounts of exemption from income tax from the present levels to $1,259 for single and $2,500 for married persons, and
(b)	By failing to remove or substantially reduce the burden of sales and excise taxes which bear most heavily on those suffering from low income and the present high cost of living.
And further, the government has failed to establish a public investment board to assure the channelling of capital investment into socially desirable projects as a means of maintaining full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living of the Canadian people.
Having moved that amendment, I think it is interesting to note that the government accepts the inevitably of depression and deliberately budgets for it. The C.C.F. believes our budget should be designed to prevent depression and to maintain the highest possible level of employment and income. Of course we shall be reminded that one attempt has been made by the government to slow down construction expenditure. How? By raising interest rates, through the withdrawal by the Bank of Canada of market support for our national bonds. But in his speech the minister said, as reported at page 4058 of Hansard:
This increase in interest rates at this time is not expected to have any great effect in restraining the high level of capital expenditure . . .
Then he went on to say:
... I do not believe that any reasonable increase in interest rates would act as a serious brake upon business expenditures under the circumstances of today, nor would it serve effectively to persuade consumers to spend less and save more of their income.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

If that is the opinion of the minister I would ask why the government took action to raise interest rates.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario discussed double depreciation. I was interested to hear him criticize double depreciation because, as far as I can recollect, these large amounts of depreciation of all kinds that have been permitted to corporations and companies, including powerful oil and mining companies, have been supported wholeheartedly by members of the party for which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario speaks. If I may give an example of the misdirection of investment I would refer the minister and the house to table 8, at page 8 of the appendix to the budget. There it is shown that, while new residential construction in 1947 increased by 37-9 per cent over 1946, other new construction increased by 59-3 per cent; new machinery and equipment, by 60-9 per cent, and investment in inventories, that is goods held for future sale, by 101-6 per cent. Housing, which I repeat should have first priority, is last in that table submitted by the minister.
My time is running out. Unlike that of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, it is not unlimited, and I do not propose to impose upon the house. Other features of the budget, however, deserve some comment. It is proposed to give further exemption of 8500 to persons over sixty-five years of age. It is difficult to understand the logic of that exemption, though we welcome it because it will benefit a few people who need more income in their declining years. But we must not forget that most of the people of Canada over the age of sixty-five will receive no benefit whatever. Indeed, forty per cent of those seventy years of age and over are today in receipt of old age pensions, indicating that their incomes are not even $750, let alone $1,500. Their incomes are less than .$600 a year. To my mind a better plan to help people of sixty-five or seventy would have been to abolish the means test, increase old age pensions to $50 a month, and at least to begin to lower the age to sixty-five, on the plan suggested in the dominion proposals to the provinces. We should not forget that the increase of $500 in the exemption will be reflected most in the highest brackets, because it will raise it at the bottom and relieve these people to that extent. So that not the needy but the more comfortably situated will reap the greatest benefit.
It is questionable whether people over sixty-five years of age need a further exemption

of $500 as much as younger people, when they are building homes, establishing businesses and raising families. Indeed, the action of the government merely strengthens our demand for an increase in the income tax exemptions by at least $500 for single persons and $1,000 for married couples, as I have indicated. If we wish to introduce new and worthwhile features into our income tax allowances we might well consider a variation of the plan adopted, I think in 1945, in the United Kingdom, under which a man working on the land may receive a further exemption of $1,000 a year if he invests that amount in improvement to his farm. The thought behind that is not unlike the thought the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario had this afternoon, except that he used it in a rather different manner than I am going to use it at the moment.
We might, for example, give an exemption to a farmer, a home-owner or a builder, that is, one who is going to inhabit the home when it is built, to the extent of an exemption of $1,000 a year, or less, up to a maximum of, we will say $10,000, spread over a period of ten or fifteen years. What we are failing to do, under present circumstances, is to encourage our people to become the owners of personal property upon which they and their families should depend for their sustenance or for the making of a good and proper home.
No party in this country, no party in the House of Commons believes more thoroughly in the right to own and enjoy personal property than the party with which I am associated. As a matter of fact, our main criticism of the present economic system is that it denies to a majority of our people the right to own homes, personal property which they and their families can enjoy. That is the main principle; that is the reason this great capitalist system under which we live has created what is sometimes called a proletariat. It is the reason for what the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario condemned and which I condemn equalty; it is the reason in many parts of the world for class warfare and class struggle, namely, the economic system which has denied to the individual the right to own the land or property upon which the happiness and sustenance of himself and his family depend.
Those of us who know the history of the rise of the industrial system, the history of the rise of capitalism from 1750, on, in Great Britain, know it was the story of the constant expropriation of the workers of Great Britain from the right to the common land and other

The Budget-Mr. Low
facilities which had been theirs for centuries after they had delivered themselves from the feudal system in vogue previously.
So we believe that the attempt should be made to distribute such property more widely; and that is one of the aims of the movement we represent in the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about private business?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Private business? Where it does not exploit the people, where it treats labour properly, and endeavours to serve the community as a whole, it requires no intervention. But when it reaches the stage of exploitation and monopoly, which private business has reached to a very large degree in our country, then it is time for the representatives of the people to take a hand.
I was going to say that even the increased penalty for failure to file income tax returns in time, suggested by the minister in his budget speech, will fall more heavily upon the farming community than upon any other group. Farmers, as we know, have great difficulty in filling out their income tax returns in time, especially as in our case those returns have to be filed in April; and the filing of income tax returns coincides with the busy seeding season of the farmers.
I believe I have exhausted the time at my disposal. May I conclude by saying this, that it was, I think, appropriate that the government should remove the tax of sixty cents a gallon on vinegar. It will at least remind the Canadian people of a budget that is thoroughly sour.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, it has been indeed a delightful experience to listen to the two splendid speeches we have heard this afternoon, particularly in relation to a budget which has been variously described as an umbrella budget, a vinegar budget, an alarm clock budget. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not have to provide the people of Canada with alarm clocks to waken them to the fact that his budget is a dreary document, without a ray of sunshine, and entirely lacking in faith and optimism.
Upon his very good presentation of what I thought was a very bad case, I offer to the minister my congratulations. I think a good deal of my hon. friend. I have been very fond of him ever since I came to the house and learned to know him. I am sorry, therefore, that I cannot go any further in my congratulations today.
As I listened the other night to the presentation of the government's financial pro-5849-271
gram for the ensuing year, it became perfectly clear that the minister was unfolding before us what one might expect from mentalities geared to traditions of scarcity.
The successive budgets presented to parliament since confederation, and more particularly those of the past twenty-five years, have all conformed to a single general pattern. Each has been simply another link added to the ball and chain which the years of financial misrule have forged about the feet of the Canadian people. This budget could not have been better calculated to hold the citizens of this country fettered in their struggle for happiness, limited in their exercise of normal freedom, and frustrated in their just claim to reasonable material security.
The budget now before us is no exception to that general rule. It is another ball-and-chain budget. Over the years the weight of the ball has become heavier, the links of the chain bigger and tougher. And the minister had better begin to notice that the protests and groans of the Canadian people are becoming louder and much more insistent.
The minister at this time could have brought financial proposals before parliament that would have cut the chains loose, once and for all, so that neither ball nor chain could ever again shackle the Canadian economy. But in his fear of full production he missed the chance and muffed the ball.
I suppose it is a foregone conclusion that a majority of the members of this parliament, each elected by the voters of his constituency and responsible to them, will accept the minister's budget; will commit this parliament to its adoption. No budget presented by any government has ever been materially altered, much less defeated, in the history of our parliament. That very tradition serves to bind the ball and chain more firmly on to our people and their economy.
I have just wondered if, in this fourth session of Canada's twentieth parliament, faced with some realization of the extent to which the monstrous ball and chain bind us down, a majority of the members of this house would show courage to ignore that tradition; and with a consciousness of their responsibilities to their electors transcending all party considerations, accept proposals counter to some of those in the budget, but designed to help the Canadian people to realize that happy condition wherein they might be unfettered in their pursuit of happiness and not frustrated in their struggle for reasonable material security. With the minister's budget before them, how else could the average run of Canadian feel than frustrated and the
The Budget-Mr. Low

average Canadian businessman than discouraged? The general attitude is, I think, admirably summed up by Walter D. Jones, president of the Canadian chamber of commerce, in these words:
The government's financial policy seems to be based on the questionable assumption that money in its own hands will be spent wisely and well, but money, in the hands of a citizen or a businessman must be heavily taxed for fear of its becoming a danger to the national economy. Experience shows no justification for such an assumption.
Indeed, when the finance minister states in the face of the largest surplus in the country's history that he must put still more money away for a rainy day, he must surely know- that it is equally important that tax rates, even in good times, should not be confiscatory to the point of preventing the thrifty taxpayer himself from saving money for a rainy day.
I close the quotation at that point. I say that is my sentiment exactly. Most Canadians are becoming wiser with regard to finance and taxes than the minister appears to give them credit for. For instance, they know it is sheer nonsense for the federal government to pretend that it is putting away money for a rainy day. If the minister had declared that he was putting into storage material things like not easily perishable foodstuffs, defence materials and such like out of present production against the day when these things might be short, then it would have made sense, but if the government puts away a whole shipload of money, when the rainy day comes the real comfort to both government and people would be the production of labour and machines, and not the money.
The Minister of Finance at any time can get all the money this country needs to distribute both current and accumulated production without having to save that money from one year to the next. But not so with the individual, not so with the businessman. Moreover, if the government is in real earnest about debt reduction I suggest that there is a far more effective way of considering it than by practising highway robbery on the producers of wealth in this country. This I shall refer to very soon.
Right now I think is the time to revive the hope of our people and the faith that their productive efforts and thrift will be rewarded by a government that is determined to provide them with ample opportunity for the abundant life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. To achieve these ends, I submit counter-proposals to some of those that have been submitted to this house by the minister. I propose that a national monetary authority be set up at once, responsible to parliament and vested with powers in the name of the

people of Canada to enable the following physically possible results to become financially possible.
First, I propose, as an initial step in a comprehensive debt-retirement program, that Canada's national debt be forthwith reduced by $3,500 million to $4,000 million. This to be done under a procedure wherein the monetary authority shall call upon the chartered banks to deliver to the Bank of Canada the Dominion of Canada securities which they hold up to that value, each bank to be credited on the books of the Bank of Canada with an amount equal to the face value of the securities delivered by it as an asset to balance the liabilities of the said bank to its depositors. The national monetary authority will then so regulate the use of this credit as to enable the chartered banks to meet their liabilities to their depositors in an orderly fashion and in a manner to maintain the stability of the national economy. This initial move will save to the people of Canada not less than $100 million annually in interest.
Second, I accept the provisions for expenditure as submitted by the minister in his estimates. These may be revised as discussion in the committee of supply may indicate as desirable. But in addition, I propose provision for expenditures as follows:
(A)	Cancellation of the existing reduction in family allowances for each child after the fourth. This to be the first step toward an ultimate increase of fifty per cent in all family allowances as soon as Canada's production has reached an optimum level and conditions of foreign aid and world trade make it possible. I estimate that this provision will require an additional $15,000,000.
(B)	1 Immediate provision for old age pensions of $50 a month at seventy years without a means test, this to be the first in a series of steps to be taken toward the objective of a $50 pension at age sixty. Succeeding steps to be taken also as Canadian production expands toward its optimum level and when international trade and foreign recovery assistance problems yield to successful solution. I estimate that this provision will require an additional $169,000,000 from the federal government.
(C)	Pensions, for needy widows of sixty years and over, and payments to all disabled adults not otherwise provided for by government allowances, no matter what the cause of disability, if any, at age eighteen years. I think this will require approximately $20,000,000.

The Budget-Mr. Low
(D)	Provision for a sum for the bringing up of war veterans allowances from $30 to $50 a month for single persons and from $60 to $85 a month for married persons and to increase 100 per cent disability pensions to $100 a month. This will require an additional $10,000,000.
(E)	Provision for the encouragement, by subsidy or otherwise, of the increased production of primary products whose importation into this country from the United States has caused such a shortage of United States dollars. The objective must be to make Canada in the shortest possible time as self-sufficient as is possible in such things as sugar, coal and steel. For this purpose I would set aside $75,000,000.
These five proposals for additional expenditures total $289,000,000. They could be provided for entirely out of the surplus which the minister has estimated. The extent to which that surplus was intended for debt reduction becomes of very little consequence since I have already provided for the reduction of debt to the extent of $3,500 million to $4,000 million, with a consequent saving in interest of $100,000,000 to $120,000,000 a year.
On the revenue side I propose that the sales tax be abolished. The minister estimates an income of $395 million, in round figures, from this source; hence reduction in revenue if this proposal were adopted would be $395 million. Abolition of the sales tax must be accompanied by measures to ensure that the benefits are passed on to consumers in lower prices. One such measure is suggested later when I deal with corporation income tax. Since this tax, like all hidden or indirect taxes, has the effect of pyramiding costs, it can be reasonably expected that the cost of living would soon show a much greater reduction than eight per cent as a result of its abolition.
I propose the cancellation of the recently imposed excise tax of twenty-five per cent, and that it be replaced by import restrictions as long as it is necessary to take unusual measures to safeguard our dollar reserves.
In the income tax field, Social Crediters have consistently pressed for raising of exemptions to $3,000 and $2,000. As the first move in this direction, I propose that exemptions be raised this year to $1,500 for single persons and to $2,400 for married persons, and that that portion of incomes in excess of $3,000 be taxed for the coming year on a basis beginning at forty per cent, with a rising scale, so that the loss of revenue from this source should not exceed $300 million.
Corporate income tax requires considerable adjustment if proper incentives to all-out production are to be provided, and if we are to
5849-271J
ensure the passing on to consumers of benefits resulting from sales tax abolition. Therefore I propose exemption from corporate income tax on a basis that would represent ten per cent return on capital, this figure to be arrived at by a procedure similar to that used by the board of referees, formerly set up and used by the Minister of Finance; this exemption to be conditional upon the corporation furnishing satisfactory evidence that savings in cost resulting from sales tax abolition have been passed on to consumers. Moreover, I propose that corporate incomes in excess of the ten per cent just outlined, but not exceeding twenty per cent, be taxed sixty per cent; and all corporate profits over twenty per cent on capital invested be taxed at the rate of eighty per cent. I estimate that on this basis the yield in taxes would be about the same as that estimated by the minister on the basis of forty per cent of all corporate income, as provided in the budget before the house. I might say, in passing, that it would reveal a more healthy state of affairs if there were hardly any revenue on this basis. It would mean that corporations would have succeeded in so organizing their affairs that, after dealing fairly and equitably with their employees and customers, they had managed to arrived at a just and satisfactory profit, and no more. In such an event, what I set out hereafter will take care of the eventuality of loss of revenue on this count, should we experience that happy outcome. I should just say here, that ten per cent profit is not excessive. A ten per cent book profit generally permits but a five per cent distribution, the balance usually being plowed back for capital purposes.
All these proposals represent a decrease in revenue amounting to $695 million, without allowance for possible reduction in income as a result of the corporate income tax changes suggested. Then, when we add the proposed additional expenditures of $289 million, we find in my proposals a total upset in the minister's budget calculations of some $984 million.
I recommend that this amount of $984 million be provided for as follows:
(a)	by using from the estimated surplus- $484 million.
(b)	by saving in interest charges through the debt reduction which I outlined at the beginning-$100 million.
(c)	by estimated increases in revenue from remaining sources of taxation, over and above calculations by the minister, which are bound to result from increased buoyancy in the national economy-$100 million.
(d)	by use of national credit through the Bank of Canada-$300 million.
<260
The Budget-Mr. Low

Hon. members are at once in a position, it seems to me, to appraise the extent to which my proposals will bring about a large measure of those results which the people desire, and which the manpower and resources of this great nation can unquestionably achieve. They implement some of the possibilities of the true economic situation, and start us on the road to peaceful prosperity for every Canadian. Because they are based on true economic principles, they can bring to Canadians a great degree of security and an ever-increasing measure of freedom. So long as they can be implemented, there can be no argument against them, except perhaps that they do not go far enough in the constructive and progressive set-up of which they form but the first steps.
In giving them consideration, hon. members will naturally require an answer to the question : Will their adoption mean aggravated inflation? The limited time at my disposal prevents me from developing the answer to that question at this time. One of my colleagues who will follow' in this debate will deal with this question fully. Just let me say in passing that the adoption of my budget proposals need not, and very likely will not, aggravate inflationary tendencies already present. I propose that any threat of aggravated inflation be effectively dealt with, whether under my proposals or under the budget the minister has brought before us. I do not like inflation any more than anyone else. It can be controlled, and I say that inherent in the proposals I have made are the controlling factors against inflation.
Surely hon. members can visualize, in the exercise of a single thought, the transformation which the adoption of these proposals will bring to our problems of production. Consider the incentive which industrial management will find in a realization that profits to the extent of ten per cent will not be subject to confiscation in any degree. To this extent, at least, the industrial producer becomes a free agent, unmolested by all the annoyances and costs of bureaucratic interference.
Consider for a moment the new incentive to the married workman who earns $2,400 or less, and who knows his pay envelope will come to him intact and unmolested by the high-handed exactions of a toll of "deducts". He will be conscious that his weekly pay envelope will secure for him and his family something more on a par with his productive effort, because of the removal of those ugly hidden taxes that breed high prices and constitute a burden on those in the lower income brackets out of all proportion to any added service the government may render as a result of the proceeds of their collection.

I am convinced that the removal of the sales tax and special excise tax, aided by the increased production that is bound to result from the improved incentive, can in a short time lower the cost of living index from its all-time high of 152 to less than 130, and in longer time to normal.
Consider the new spirit and the will-to-do that would come from a sure knowledge that, as effective productive effort increases the volume of goods and services available, children will be provided for through increased family allowances, on a basis that means a substantial contribution to what it takes these days to meet the essential material needs of a child; the aged, disabled and widowed will be cared for in comfort and in some degree of decent living. It does not require prophetic vision to see ahead, my proposals drying up the cesspools of hardship and discontent in which communism thrives. It needs no exaggerated imagination to see ahead a new atmosphere for constructive, friendly relations between labour and management, such as to ensure the production of wanted goods and services at an ever-increasing pace.
Inflation will not follow the adoption of our proposals. They have in them what can be used to curb the excessive forces that bring on inflation. Above all, they have in them the spur necessary to induce greater and greater production of wanted goods and services. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, that item of $75,000,000 to encourage increased production of such items as sugar beets, coal and steel represents the most effective possible attack on the threat to the Canadian economy from an unwarranted dependence on products from the United States and other dollar countries which has resulted in the austerity program now in effect in Canada.
You have before you my proposals for a bountiful budget as opposed to the baleful ball-and-chain effort of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. In my proposals, adjustments may be needed in matters of detail and in connection with accidental circumstances which I have not considered. I have not at my disposal for research and preparation the minister's bevy of personnel. I often feel that he w'ould be a whole lot better off without his, or most of them. Too many of them are steeped in the mentality of scarcity' of the London School of Economics, where for now almost a century journeymen economists have learned to forge the ball and chain. But the framework is there. I have not been able and shall not be in the time at my disposal to present full arguments and supporting statements, but others will follow from this corner
The Budget-Mr. Low

of the house who will present those supporting statements. I submit that, contrasted with the succession of ball-and-chain budgets placed before this parliament in the past, our proposals represent the transition from a long, dark night to the dawn of a new day whose span, by the way, can be just what we make it. Our proposals at least begin to place the proper value on our human resources, the greatest resource that we have in Canada, and a resource which we very often overlook and fail to develop.
I think most hon. members will recognize that the proposals I have made are designed to implement what was contained in the amendment which my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), twice submitted in the throne speech debate. These amendments called for the application of Social Credit principles which our group have been expounding in this parliament over the past thirteen years. The things I have suggested were also involved in the amendment which I submitted to the throne address last year, which amendment included these words:
The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services, and as a guarantee that this country would not again be subjected to financial depression, to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry.
When I moved that amendment in 1947, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) gave support to that portion of my amendment just quoted, with certain limitations. But the limitations did not exclude anything that was involved in my amendment of a year ago, or indeed anything in my present proposals. I quote the opposition leader's exact words on that occasion as taken from Hansard:
To the extent that such a fiscal policy has been or may be used for the support of definite public services such as old age pensions, family allowances, floor prices and so on, services that are regarded as being essential to the public good, to that degree I support it.
Mr. Speaker, those words of the hon. leader of the opposition exactly fit the proposals I have made today, because I have called for the use of the national credit for family allowances, old age pensions, floor prices, and so on. Such use of the national credit to the amount of $300 million means that purchasing power to that extent would circulate amongst the people without creating a debt at its source and without accumulating an interest burden throughout its whole life. It
need never be cancelled out of existence until that day when production falls short of the purchasing power available in this country.
I visualize for the national monetary authority, which it is proposed to set up, a role ever-increasing in importance. Its main function would be to implement the financial policy laid down for it by this parliament, a policy designed to keep always in the hands of all the people sufficient effective purchasing power to balance the total prices of the goods and services available for sale-no more and no less. Let me emphasize here that in it would be no element of that bureaucratic control which, till now, has been increasing its grip on this nation. Moreover,
I have no idea for the present or the future that the chartered banks shall in any way be interfered with in the excellent accounting job they are doing and the skilled judgment they are exercising in the financing of production. I simply advocate that the sovereign title to the creation of money be vested in the people whose inalienable possession it must be, and must remain. There is very little-wrong with the present method of financing: production, but there is everything wrong: with the financing of consumption, which seems to be nobody's job these days.
At the same time, I should like to assure hon. members that in the proposals I have made this afternoon the depositors in chartered banks of this country will not be interfered with in any way in the control of their own deposits. They shall continue to control them and to use them as they so desire.
With reference to this inalienable right of the people to exercise effective control of currency and credit, I find myself in complete agreement with the cogent pronouncement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which he made in a radio address just before he came into power in 1935, repeated and printed in a pamphlet calculated to help bring him to power, but on which he has been strangely silent ever since. I quote:
Let me repeat what I said in parliament: once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament, and democracy, is idle and futile.
I am sure the Prime Minister agrees withi that statement even today. I am glad that he is in his seat, and I am glad to see him: nodding his head in assent to what I have-said. In the light of that and of what I have said this afternoon, knowing the hearts of a good many of the Liberal members, I
Supply-Agriculture

think I should expect substantial support for my proposals from the Liberal side of the house, including the Prime Minister. I realize, sir, that the rules of this house prevent me from formally submitting my proposals for a vote in this debate. Not more than two amendments can be submitted on the budget, but it does seem to me that the people of this nation are entitled to know the extent to which their representatives are prepared to support or to reject the proposals I have made. It should not be by the application of house rules that this nation is governed, although I recognize that rules are necessary in carrying on the nation's business in this parliament. I suggest that if the majority of the members of this parliament desire during this session to give effect to our proposed financial changes, it is entirely within their power to do so. If the majority of the members want to do these things, I feel sure that the minister who has submitted this budget, and of whom I am very fond, as I have already said, could be prevailed upon to insert the necessary changes which would give effect to the things I have proposed.
Let me say this. I am convinced that if the minister will do just that, if he will revise his budget along these lines, I am satisfied that it will receive support in the house unparalleled in the history of this parliament. I cannot resist the temptation to say that his political fortunes, and the fortunes of those associated with him, would be enhanced to a degree that will never be achieved at any national convention such as is proposed for next August.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that in the name of my constituents, yes, in the name of every citizen of this country, I call upon this parliament to rise up now and cast off the ball and chain and consign them forever to oblivion.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OP CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief. When the hon. member sponsoring this bill introduced it on February 27, if I had been in possession of the information I now have, which was given when the bill was being considered in committee, perhaps I would have changed my mind in some respects. When I rose to speak at that time, what I had in mind was to obtain for Ontario, if possible, the assurance that was given to British Columbia on May 2, 1947, in connection with a similar bill, by the hon. member for New Westminster in reply to a question asked by my deskmate, the hon. member for Vancouver South. Let me read what was said. The hon. member for Vancouver South said:
I think it is essential that some protection should be given to telephone users of British Columbia. I understand that the hon. member has been authorized to give assurance to the effect that the company has no present intention of applying for an increase of rates and will not make any such application unless compelled to do so by extensive changes in conditions.
The hon. member for New Westminster replied:
That is my definite understanding.
That is what I had in mind when I spoke on February 27 last; I wanted some assurance in connection with the present bill. This matter was considered by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines on May 11. One of the witnesses was Mr. N. A. Munnoch, K.C., vice-president and general counsel for the company. Referring to the amount of money which was to be spent, the hon. member for The Battlefords asked:
Can you make that expenditure and hold your present toll rate at the present figure?
That was a very pertinent question, and in reply Mr. Munnoch said:
It is impossible to say what will happen to telephone rates, but I can say that at the present time the company has filed no application with the railway board for an increase in rates-
Then he added:
-and has made no preparation for filing such an application.
If that assurance had been given by the sponsor of the bill I for one, at any rate, might have taken a different position, though I am glad I took the position I did at that time. Then Mr. Munnoch went further and said:
We have carried on through the war period and by reason of economies and technological improvements in telephony we have been able to maintain our present rate structure since it was established in 1926.
They did that all through the depression and all through the war, and I was convinced that they must have exercised very good management, particularly, in order to have $13,000,000 left from the $75,000,000 by which they were authorized to increase their capital on the last occasion. So I must confess I am convinced that the Bell Telephone Company when it issues this stock will spend the money judiciously. I also have in mind the reply by the vice-president and general counsel, which to me is a little stronger than if the statement had been made by the hon. member for Outremont, and which is equal to the statement made by the hon. member for New Westminster when the British Columbia telephone bill was under consideration. All these factors induce me to refrain from further opposition to the bill, and I propose to vote for it.
Just before resuming my seat, I wish to compliment my hon. friends to the left on the stand they took. Along with others and myself in this party, including the hon. member for Broadview, the hon. member for High Park and the hon. member for Vancouver South, they did what they thought was their duty. I am never afraid to do what I think is my duty. I am under obligation to no living man, as far as I know. I have no stock in the Bell Telephone Company, and further I can say this, which I have not said before. When I came to this house I divested myself of any stock I had in any concern or company with which I had anything to do that I thought might ever come to this house for a favour or for support. I wanted to be in the position that I was under no obligation to anyone who might come here. What I have
Bell Telephone Company

said or done has been from my heart. It may have been wrong as far as my head is concerned, but it has come from my heart and I believe it has been right. So I compliment my hon. friends to the left, because in my opinion they were rather meanly treated by reason of the epithets and phrases which were hurled at them and which they did not deserve. They did what they thought was their duty, and I share with them the assurance I quoted given by the general counsel and vice-president of the Bell Telephone Company. That is what I was after. As you well know, Mr. Chairman, in my riding are perhaps twenty thousand, more or less, Bell Telephone users. In the main they are humble people, and I was anxious that they should not be asked to pay more than the $3.45 a month they are now paying. I accept the assurance of the vice-president of the company in that regard.
In conclusion, may I ask the hon. member for Outremont to communicate to the company that I for one would strongly recommend that they do what they did on the last occasion, at the instance of the hon. member for Broadview. No man I know in public life has done more for his constituents than that hon. gentleman. On the last occasion he fought a hard battle against all sorts of cruel opposition, for which he received no thanks whatever, to obtain a flat rate not only for Toronto but for the people living all around and about it. I would suggest to the hon. member for Outremont that an effort be made to get that flat rate for an area within five miles of the hon. member's own city, the city of Toronto and other large cities. It seems to me that it is not fair to ask suburban residents just outside cities to pay rates that are higher than those which we pay in the cities.
Further, I wish to express my appreciation of what has been done by the hon. member for High Park. I have always found him a fearless fighter. I would say the same for the hon. member for Vancouver South, and I pay my tribute to them for the part they have played in bringing about the assurance given re rates.
I fully realize that if, in time, for one cause or another the company has to have a higher rate, it will maj<e its application to the railway board. I am satisfied with the assurance that was given to the hon. member for Vancouver South on May 2, 1947, and as above referred to re this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this group is opposed to this section of the bill, and to the bill of which this is a section. We base

our opposition chiefly upon the opinion held generally by ourselves and at least by some members in all parts of the house, that the increase in capitalization asked for by the company is too high.
The company is asking that its capitalization be increased from the present amount of $150,000,000 to $500,000,000. We believe that is too large an amount of capitalization for the company to ask at any one time. We believe, too, that a company with a capitalization of that sort, and particularly a transportation company-because, in a way, it is a transportation company-by its very nature would become a virtual monopoly. We believe that if it is to become a monopoly it should be a monopoly owned by the people of this country.
We could have a telephone company operated on a co-operative basis, in which event the profit would go back to the users of the telephone, or we could have a publicly owned company, in which case those dividends would go to all the people of the provinces in which the company performs its operations.
In this instance the profits of the company do not go to the users of the telephone as such. They go to those fortunate people who in early days invested their money in this venture. We have no great fault to find with that, under present circumstances. But we do recognize that the assets of this great company have been built up by the users of those public facilities. They have created those assets, but they are in the position of not owning any of them.
Dealing again with our view that the increase in capitalization is too great, let me say that this, like other companies, is one which has to come to parliament from time to time to obtain increases in its capitalization. I shall have a word or two to say about that later.
This group delayed the bill in its early stages, but only until two conditions were fulfilled. We held it up, first, until it had been established that there had been good and sufficient time for hon. members to say practically everything which could be said in respect of the bill, and time in which all information available could be obtained. In the second place, we held up the bill until we discovered that in the house a majority of members-and I believe this to be true-were in favour of an increased capitalization for this company.
When those two conditions had been fulfilled we withdrew our opposition and allowed the bill to go to the appropriate committee. I was a member of that committee and, if I had

Bell Telephone Company
the time and were in the mood, I might be somewhat critical of committees of that sort. We had a genial and good-natured chairman- perhaps that was part of the difficulty. I would say in passing that it is unfortunate for a small minority on a committee when the greater number on the committee are in favour of rushing legislation through. On at least twTo occasions I was on my feet in an effort to move an amendment to the section we are now discussing, but I was informed that it had been carried long ago. My voice was not heard among the vociferous chorus of "carried, carried, carried", from all sides, which reminded me collectively of the individual voice of the former minister of veterans affairs.

In the committee we met the officers of the company. May I pay tribute to them by saying that they were fair.
I found some fault with them in that they would not make certain prophecies which I tried to persuade them to make. However, I believe they did produce the facts, to our satisfaction. We would like to persuade those officers to be content with a little less capitalization than is called for in this section.
After having examined the witnesses as best we could, we did not alter our conviction that the capitalization asked for is still too high. And we are also alarmed by the other point brought out by the hon. member for Davenport, namely, that we are likely to be faced with a rise in telephone rates charged by the company.
In its final analysis the money asked for in this section is needed for a tremendous expansion of the company in the matter of giving new service. That means practically the installation of new telephones and the setting up of machinery to service those telephones. This great amount of money could be defined, roughly, as the number of new units necessary multiplied by the cost of the telephone unit.
Before taking my seat, I shall have further comment to make on that aspect of the matter *-the same comment I made in committee. I learned from questioning the officials that the company estimates that at the present time the cost of installing a telephone unit at present prices is $550. One member of the committee seemed confused on this; he appeared to think the cost of the mouthpiece was the main factor. I believe my information goes farther than that.
Might I point out that that figure of $550 is an all-time high. I asked the officials for corresponding prices of installations and the cost of a telephone unit in times when prices were not so high. I believe the official mentioned the period between 1932 and 1937 and gave the figure of $230. which may or may not have been the lowest figure in that period. The officials did not know. I want to make the point that the amount asked for is predicated upon the price per unit remaining as it is now or going higher. I do not think the company is justified in the assumption that the price will stay as it is or go up during the next five or six years.
I would remind hon. gentlemen that prices have been known to go down before, and drastically. If prices were to go back to the $230 figure the company would then have a much higher capitalization than it needed and would find itself in possession of vast sums of money which for the moment were not needed for the expansion of the company.
I shall here refer to the minutes of proceedings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where I am reported on page 44 as follows:
Mr. Knight:	The position is this: if your
cost goes down to $230 within the next year or so, you will find yourselves, in terms of what you are asking for, in the position of having twice the amount you need, predicated on present costs?
Mr. Johnston:	I think we can agree with
that.
This company must come to parliament once in a while, and I think that is a healthy condition. I believe I used the expression that they must come for an occasional medical check-up. If my argument is sound and prices go down it will mean that this company will not have to come to parliament for an increase in its capitalization for perhaps twice as long a period. That is one reason why we think the amount asked for is too great, and we hope that the company and this committee will be satisfied with a lesser amount. I think that to decrease the amount asked for would be to the advantage of all the people of Canada, and so I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke):
That subsection 1 of section 1 of an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada be amended by striking out the word "five" as it appears in line 26 of the said section and substituting therefor the word "three."

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in connection with the amendment which has been moved by my colleague. This company is seeking a substantial increase in its capitalization, and I submit that a company which is admittedly a monopoly should satisfy this committee that it needs that amount of capital. The onus of proof is on the company to show that it needs an expansion of $350,000,000 in its capital.
Bell Telephone Company

I contend that the amount for which the company asks is excessive, and I base my argument entirely upon the brief presented by the company and upon the evidence given before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
According to the brief and according to the evidence, the company expended $104,495,000 between August 1, 1945, and the end of March, 1948, in order to instal 329,000 additional telephones, an increase of 32 per cent. This means that in a little over two and half years the company expended in capital funds $317.60 for each telephone installed. This sum represents the cost of the following capital equipment: right of way, land and buildings, central office equipment, station equipment, exchange lines, toll lines and general equipment.
The company stated in its brief and its officers said in their evidence that it requires this capital expansion in order to instal during the next five years an additional 455,000 telephones. According to the experience of the company in the last two and a half years, which I submit is a recent period, the cost of each telephone to be installed is S317.60. On that experience the capital expenditure required in the next five years for 455,000 telephones would be $144,508,000. When the officer of the company who seemed to be giving evidence on technical matters was questioned on this he said that $317.60 was too low, that it would be around $500, and later on he increased the amount to $550. According to the answers he gave to me, I suggest that this was a pure estimate, which seems to me to be too high in the light of the company's recent experience which showed that a telephone cost $317.60.
Even assuming the cost to be $500, during the next five years the company would expend $227,500,000 in order to instal 455.000 telephones, not the $350,000,000 it is asking for. It was stated in the brief of the company that it still has $13,000,000 of treasury stock from the $150,000,000 which is authorized at the present time. Deducting that amount from the $227,500,000 shows that the company would need only $214,500,000 of capital during the next five years in order to make the proposed1 expansion.
According to the evidence and according to the brief, it is indicated that not all the money which the company will require will be raised through the issue of capital stock. The evidence and the brief show that a substantial portion of it, about one-half, is expected to be obtained, and I quote:
. . . through borrowings and other available resources of the company such as depreciation credits which will be used and invested in the plant to be constructed.

Therefore, according to that plan, the company would need to raise by sale of shares only one-half of the $214,500,000. namely, $107,250,000.
It would seem to me that an increase in capital of $150 million would amply meet the needs of the company for the next five years. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the company has not discharged the burden of proof that it needs this $500 million; that is to say, an extra $350 million, and I think we would be remiss in our duty if we were to grant an increase of $350 million on such flimsy evidence as we had in the committee.

subtopic: BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OP CANADA
speechtext:
I wish to speak for five or six minutes on this bill respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. I wanted to speak before the amendment was moved. I wish to point out that I am not a socialist in the ordinary sense. Four or five years ago when the Postmaster General's estimates were up I urged that we should follow the practice in England where the telephone is a branch of the Post Office Department, because our rates were very high. In my opinion a residence telephone should not cost more than $15 or $20 and a business telephone in the neighbourhood of $45.
We had an investigation of railway, express, and telephone companies conducted by the Drayton-Acworth commission some years ago. Sir Henry Drayton was the chairman, Mr. Acworth was a British engineer, and the other member of the commission was Mr. A. H. Smith, president of the New York Central. What did they report? They reported that any application for an increase in capitalization should first be reported on by the board of railway commissioners, now the board of transport commissioners. I believe that such a report should have been obtained in this case, and that is my first objection to this bill.
The stock of this company is quoted today at 162J. If the company gets the increase in capitalization I believe that the stock will immediately go to about 200. The company cannot pay dividends of eight per cent on that high capitalization, without an immediate rate increase. I am opposed to over-capitalization of these companies. We had the same arguments presented when the cheap light and power movement started in Ontario, and there were the same attacks on public men, but cheap light and power was a boon not only to the urban centres but also to the rural communities in this province.
Over-capitalization immediately means an increase in rates, and if this increase goes through, telephone service will cost three times as much as it should. The telephone is a pub-

Bell Telephone Company
lie utility. I have no mandate from the people I represent to vote for this increase and create a monopoly. Monopolies are flourishing like a green bay tree in this country at the present time, and there is no one to stop them. Monopolies started about the time of Queen Elizabeth. She gave the sole right to trade in certain commodities to a few people, and that principle has been extended in modem times, so that many groups of persons and corporations enjoying a monopoly have the power to enhance prices in conformity with their own purposes.
It is for the railway commission to find out whether there is need for competition in the telephone field. I say yes. and competition should be welcomed by the people of our province. Are we getting telephone service at cost now? No. The people in Britain do, through the British post office department.
In Cochrane the cost of power went to $60 per horsepower.

speechtext:
I am going to support the amendment, Mr. Chairman. I have no mandate from the people of the province of Ontario or from my constituents to continue a monopoly of half a billion dollars. There is practically no regulation of this company. Why did it go to another place with this bill, where the fee is only $200 as compared with $500 in this chamber? I do not know whether the house understands that. The Bell Telephone company is a good company, well conducted, and I would like to see it get all the capital it needs to meet its capital requirements for the next ten or twenty years, but I think an increase in the capitalization of 100 per cent, bringing it to $300 million, would be ample for many years to come.
It took almost a motion in the house to try to get a stenographic report of the proceedings in the other place with respect to this bill. I am not blaming the company or the mover of the bill for that, because I think the mover of the bill wanted us to have the report Why should we not know all the ins and outs of this
application? If we had had a stenographic report of the proceedings in the other place it would have saved five or six nights of discussion in this house.
I do not believe that we should support this bill and create a monopoly by raising the capitalization to half a billion dollars. One clause of the bill gives the board of transport commissioners jurisdiction to say what tne amount shall be, but you have to be a shareholder before you can get the board to deal with that matter.
In the mother country they are having the very same discussions. The party which is called Conservative over there wanted to refer allegations about monopolies to an independent commission. We have a regulatory commission in this country, but they do not regulate. In Great Britain they rejected the United States idea of controlling monopolies by charging them with "restraint of trade" under the provisions of their anti-trust legislation, which can be enforced in the law courts. In the United States they have the interstate commerce commission over there and it is a very long and expensive proceeding. The result is these monopolies, cartels and things are international. They have entered this country, as hon. members know.
As I see it, it is the function and duty of the board of transport commissioners to find out the facts about this particular company. Do they need half a billion dollars, or will an increase of $300 million or $150 million tide them over for the next ten or fifteen years? I say yes, I believe it will. I suggest that the board of transport commissioners should find out the following facts about this particular company. If it is a monopoly, is it harmful, and why? If it is, what should be done about it? In dealing with this application I believe that the House of Commons would like the board of transport commissioners to consider that fact. Second, it is satisfactory up to half a billion dollars, or would $300 million do for ten or fifteen years? If not, what improvements or suggestions would the board of transport commissioners demand of this company? Is the telephone a monopoly? Will it have to pay dividends on half a billion dollars, or on $300 million? I believe they should find out these things in connection with this particular bill. If this bill is harmful, if it is harmful to give half a billion dollars to this company, what steps should the board of transport commissioners take to remedy the situation? They should find out whether a monopoly exists in the province. If it does, is it harmful to the public of our province and to the province of Quebec? These are a few
Bell Telephone Company

things that I think the board of transport commissioners should examine and find out.
They talk about 100,000 customers wanting telephones. Who is to blame for it? If I did not have a telephone and could not get one I could apply to the board of transport commissioners, and they would immediately, of their own volition, send an inspector around and have a proper inspection made of the application. The public do not even know that, but it could be done. I wish to say this. I stand firm on the ground that the state exists for the individual, not the individual for the state; that state interference with the full liberty of the subject is an evil thing per se, the encroachments of which should be most searchingly scrutinized and resisted ; that no government department, except where it enjoys a monopoly, can conduct a business at a profit; that the prosperity of the nation rests on the enterprise and ability of individuals in free association to conduct their affairs with a minimum of regulation and interference; that capital and labour are partners and not enemies, indispensable to one another; that bureaucracy is the enemy of them both and will ruin them morally and financially if they do not restrict its inordinate increase; and, finally, that what I seek is the welfare of the whole community, and no sectional or class advantage.
I believe that is the doctrine which would be acceptable to the people. I appreciate the fact that this company and its officers may have given good satisfaction. I believe they are asking over-capitalization in regard to a utility which belongs to our province.
I have always been in favour of the public ownership of the telephone. I proposed that many years ago in connection with post office.
I called attention to what the post office in Britain was doing as compared with our post office, which has not made any improvements since confederation except in regard to the mail and all that kind of thing.

Science service-
5. Science service administration, $168,374.

Before the dinner recess the hon. member for Mackenzie was asking some questions with regard to the professional classes, particularly the scientists, in the Department of Agriculture. I presume the hon. member had in mind the science services all the way through the department rather than just those in the science branch itself. I should like to make a general statement as to the position, and then, if there are any questions to be asked with regard to the experimental farms or otherwise, they can be dealt with as we come to the particular items.
The general salary adjustments for the Department of .Agriculture have been completed. Individual cases which could not be handled in the general revision, and some anomalies arising out of the revision, are now being adjusted as individual cases. In the professional classes the increases varied from $300 to $600 per annum, depending upon revisions which had been made during the previous two years. In other words, we started making these revisions in 1945. In some cases revisions had been made previously and in other cases they had not, so that there is a variation between S300 and $600, depending upon whether revisions had been made on a prior occasion.
During the time the general revision has been in progress the reclassification of individuals who have assumed increased responsibilities has continued, and consequently many employees have had their salaries increased by from $480 to $900 over the 1945 levels, by a combination of the general revision and a specific reclassification. Practically all the professional employees of the department have now benefited, and individual cases are being dealt with as I indicated a few moments ago.

I wonder if under this item the minister is in a position to say what is happening to the pine trees of this country Many of them appear to be turning brown. Does his department have anything to do with that?

The main difficulty is a disease known as white pine blister rust, which has been affecting the trees. A study is being made in an attempt to combat it.
Will the trees die in time if the condition is not remedied?

Yes, it will kill the trees eventually. I am not in a position to say just how long it will take, because the period varies in different places and under different conditions. If the ravages are not halted, it will kill the trees eventually.
Has it increased very much in the last year or two in this part of the dominion?
I am informed that there has been no marked increase, that it has been moving along at about the same rate for a considerable period of time.
Are any steps being taken to control it?
No specific way of controlling or stopping it has been developed, though continuous study and attempts to control it are being carried on.
The spruce trees in my district are going in the same way. Would it be the same disease?
The difficulty there is the spruce budworm, and an attempt is being made to control that with parasites which destroy the insect.

I brought in the director of the division on purpose to take these items tonight, but if it is important I could let one item stand when we reach it.

I should like to ask what has been done to control the blue mould which is now affecting tobacco plants in southern and western Ontario.
We have already passed that item, under plant pathology.
I thought it would come under the experimental farms.

Downy mildew or blue mould on tobacco was observed in southwestern Ontario in 1943. This was the first record for Canada. It was absent in 1944, but recurred in epidemic proportions in 1945. Thorough and quick action in getting the growers to treat their seed beds with P.D.B.- I shall not attempt to pronounce the name for which those initials stand-saved the crop. There is strong circumstantial evidence that the spores and fungus were wind-borne across lake Erie from tobacco beds or fields farther south. That is the information available.
Is P.D.B. a cure for the disease if the soil is treated?
Yes, I understand it is.
An absolute cure?

Provided that it is used
at the proper time and efficiently applied, it is a complete cure.
Has that information been conveyed to the tobacco growers? Apparently many of them are not using it.
The information has been conveyed to them, and it has been used widely. I do not know whether everyone is using it.

What is the present function of the experimental farm at Saskatoon? What particular branch of experiments is it carrying out? I understand that in the past it has been used largely in the development of young trees to be sent out to farmers in the vicinity.
The chief activities in connection with experimental work at Saskatoon are carried on at the university. The farm there is a provincial farm. We have a forestry farm.
I was referring to the forestry farm.
But there is some work being carried on at the agricultural college in connection with crops other than forestry crops. All the forage crop work is done at that plant, and the soils work.

I was wondering to what extent the forestry farm was justifying its name. To what extent are young trees grown there? Are they sent out to different farms in the district? As a matter of fact I should like to say a word for that forestry farm, because I

Supply-Agriculture
believe it is worth aJll that is being spent on it, simply through the amount of pleasure given to people who go out there to visit. On Sunday afternoons great numbers of people find it a place for pleasant recreation. I would pay tribute to the manner in which the flowerbeds and the like are kept. I was wondering, however, to what extent young trees are being developed and sent out into northern Saskatchewan.

They are going out from there at the rate of about a couple of million a year. Deciduous trees are produced at Saskatoon and coniferous trees, in so far as they are produced, are produced at Indian Head. The trees are distributed from both those farms throughout all western Canada, as a matter of fact, wherever they are required. They are going out in the numbers I indicated a moment ago.

The minister will recall that sometime ago the board of trade of Dauphin made certain representations to his department in connection with an experimental farm which they thought would be most desirable in the Dauphin area. If I remember the correspondence correctly, the reply was that at this time it was not thought advisable to establish an experimental farm in that area.
Last year, I believe it was, when the estimates of the minister were up for consideration, the minister made a statement to the effect that in his opinion it would be a desirable project in that part of Manitoba. I would draw to his attention that we have no experimental farm in that large agricultural section of the province, and I would hope that the minister has not closed the door on the idea that perhaps in the future he would consider setting up an experimental farm at Dauphin or in that district.

There is no experimental farm there, and there is no provision in these estimates for putting one there. I am not in a position to say that we are likely to do so in the near future. However, some fine work is being done there by Mr. Parker. I was up there last summer and visited the experimental plots he is operating, and I believe it is among the best work being done in western Canada. I believe he is strongly of the opinion that good service could be rendered there by an experimental station somewhat larger than that which is there now. However, no provision is made for that in these estimates, to enlarge upon what is being done.

What is the reason for this increase? Would the minister tell the committee what has been done in the development of a rust-resistant barley?

The question which was asked just before the dinner recess, and which I answered just after the committee resumed this evening, gives the reason for a considerable portion of this increase. Many of the scientific and professional men spoken of are associated with the central experimental farm. A very considerable part of this increase is due to an increase in wages and salaries. Some of it, too, is due to studies being made, such as that just mentioned. Barley studies are being carried on here and also at Brandon and Winnipeg.
What are the types which are standing up best and which are recommended as rust-resistant? Are they malting types?

I am not in a position to give the names at the present time; but there is one malting variety and one good feed variety, both of which have been successfully developed. They are about ready for distribution.
I understood the minister to say most of this increase was due to increased salaries. I find, however, that that accounts for only $57,000.
I said a very considerable part of it.

I feel that Canadians generally are proud of the work which has been done by the director of the experimental farms service and the personnel under his supervision. This applies to the work done both in Canada and in the international field. Could the minister make some statement with regard to the progress being made in connection with the artificial insemination of horses?
There has been very little success experienced in connection with that. Experiments have been carried on at Brandon and here but without any great success.
What progress has been made in connection with Garry oats?
It is being multiplied rapidly and there has been considerable distribution both east and west.
Is that not one of the varieties susceptible to this supposedly new disease of root rot? What has been done at the experimental farms to develop an oat resistant to that disease?
It is resistant to both leaf rust and stem rust, but there is nothing to indicate that it is particularly susceptible to root rot or any disease of that kind.
It has been stated all across Canada that Garry was one of the varieties susceptible to this disease, and there should be some information from the experimental farms about this.
The gentleman who is responsible for the experimental farms has the opposite opinion and that is the only opinion I can give.

What supplies of Saunders wheat will be available in the near future?
I understand that red bobs wheat has been graded down to No. 3. As the minister knows, red bobs is grown largely in Alberta and it has been suggested that Saunders wheat will largely take its place.
It is being multiplied rapidly and distribution is being made in the northwestern section from Scott and Beaver-lodge and Lacombe.
It stands up very well?
Yes.
What is the reason for red bobs being dropped in grade from 1 to 3?

As hon. members know, wheats along with other cereals are sown on plots over a considerable part of western Canada and examined from year to year. This work is carried on under Doctor Newman. As a result of these experiments, it was found that red bobs wheat was not up to the general mark that has been made by Marquis wheat, and it has finally been displaced by Saunders, which is a good quality.

Would it be possible to delay the time when red bobs is to be declared No. 3 until ample supplies of Saunders are available? I understand that it is to be graded 3 next year. Would it be possible to put it off until 1950? There will not be sufficient supplies of Saunders wheat available until 1950.

That is not something that we can control. Grading is done under the board of grain commissioners which operates under the Department of Trade and Commerce. There is a special committee which meets every year and advises with regard to that matter. It would be better to bring the matter up on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I understand that some experimental work has been done in connection with the use of hay balers. Can the minister indicate what success if any has been achieved in the use of hay balers during the ordinary haying season in different parts of Canada?

Hay balers have always been used generally right across Canada and I do not know that anything special has been discovered recently with regard to them. It is simply a matter of having the hay in proper condition when it is baled. If it is baled under proper conditions the bales will stand up quite well, but if there is any dampness in it they will not stand up. I do not know that there is anything new with regard to balers.
What development has taken place in connection with winter wheat varieties, and I am referring to western Canada particularly?

There has been winter wheat grown in Alberta and some on the western side of Saskatchewan. From information we have here there are varieties which are not yet named but which give some promise. They are not ready for distribution and there is nothing more I can say about them
