at the moment. As is generally known, these are put through severe tests before any effort is made to multiply them and put them out, and those tests are still being made.
I understand that yobo has been grown for the last two years and that there is quite an acreage up in the southwest corner. Will that be the name of the new variety?
I do not know which variety they are using there, but I assume it is the variety that has 'been used generally through southern Alberta for some time.

Could the minister state what experimental work has been done in the production of vegetable oils? I see the hon. member for Fraser Valley is behind the curtains. I believe success has been experienced around Moose Jaw in growing rapeseed.

The seed most generally used for oil purposes in Saskatchewan and the west is rapeseed. Some work was done with sunflowers but sunflo'wers worked out more successfully in sections of Manitoba than in any other parts of the west. Then there are soya beans which do very well in the southwestern part of Ontario. We have not yet been able to develop a soya bean which will produce in the shorter seasons of the areas east and west of that. One great difficulty with the soya bean is frost, which in the spring affects the plant itself, and in the fall affects the oil-bearing qualities of the bean. So it is necessary to develop a different variety of soya bean from any we have yet, to make it possible to produce it successfully across Canada. There is one seed from which oil has been taken over a long period of time, and that is flaxseed, which is grown all over western Canada and in eastern Canada too.

I am sorry if I am dwelling too long on root rot. The minister has just said that Garry oats was not susceptible to this rot. Vicland and Beacon were two varieties that were particularly subject to this disease last year. We have had reports from officials on the seriousness of this disease and on the steps taken to protect farmers across the country against it. Work is also being done on a new variety which it is hoped would be resistant to this disease. I should like to get some information on that.

There are three commonly recognized root rot diseases, the common root rot, browning root rot, and take-all. The common root rot pathogens may attack the plant at all stages of growth, causing seedling blight, leaf spotting, head blight
and kernel smudge. The losses from these diseases are extensive during certain years in the prairie provinces, but their occurrence and the extent of their damage are so dependent on environmental conditions that it varies considerably.
To secure more accurate information on the effect of common root rot on the yield of wheat, samples were taken from selected fields in the different soil zones of Manitoba in 1939-41. The average loss was 7-5 per cent in 1939, 16-6 per cent in 1940 and 12-1 per cent in 1941; the greatest loss occurred in the southwestern part of the province.
In a similar study conducted in Saskatchewan in 194 M3, a disease rating was calculated for each field. The mean disease rating was 9-9 per cent in 1941, 6-0 per cent in 1942 and 9-4 per cent in 1943. Although the figures for Saskatchewan are not directly comparable with those for Manitoba, they indicate a seasonal fluctuation in the amount of disease, which is believed due to variations in soil, temperature and moisture.
That deals mainly with wheat in the western provinces.
It was dealing with everything affected by root rot. If my hon. friend has some information I should like him to give it to the committee.
I have heard a variety of reports and I do not know which is correct.
I have given all the information we have, but if my hon. friend has any other information we shall be glad to get it.
Could the minister not get the information?
I am not sure that the information exists. If my hon. friend will put his information on the record I shall have it looked into and see whether it is correct.
It is not my position to do that.
My position is not to give information which does not exist. The information which is in this book is all the information we have, and I cannot give any more.

I am sorry to have to refute that statement. There is other information available and I have seen it.

found profitable to grow soya beans and other oil-producing plants in the province of British Columbia due to our high cost of land and high taxes. Am I not correct in that? I do not think it has been found profitable to produce soya beans at any experimental farm in British Columbia. Is that not a fact? I think that is a fair question.

The answer I gave a few moments ago covered soils in other parts of the country. We have not yet been able to develop a soya bean which can be produced successfully in any part of Canada except the southwestern part of Ontario. I am not saying that we may not be able to develop a soya bean which can be produced profitably in other sections. In the early days we had some difficulties in connection with Red Fife wheat, which would freeze in the fall. We must find a variety of soya bean which will mature in a shorter season than any we have now. I do not know that would be true of British Columbia, but there are some conditions there which make it impossible to grow soya beans of a quality successful for oil production.

What little knowledge I have of farming is derived from the publications of the minister's department. Is it true that the growing of rapeseed and sunflower seed has been an exceedingly lucrative source of income to farmers on the prairies?

During some of the war years the growing of sunflowers, while I would not say it was very lucrative, paid its way very well, but most of those who went into the growing of sunflowers in Saskatchewan have gone out of it.
I believe many people have left Saskatchewan.

They have two reasons for that. Rapeseed has done very well in Saskatchewan and is still doing very well, but of course the government has been and still is paying a guaranteed price on rapeseed. I am not sure we have established as a fact that rapeseed can be grown in Canada in competition with, say, the Argentine or some other country. But we are doing all right with it.

Is the minister in a position to report on the progress that has been made in the last two years in establishing an illustration station in the immediate vicinity of the Red river valley south of Winnipeg? There is an experimental station not far off

at Morden, but the soil in the immediate vicinity of the Red river is of quite a different type from that at Morden, and I think an illustration station on the eastern side would go a long way toward transplanting there the benefits that have been obtained at the Morden experimental station. Is the minister in a position to make a statement on that?

Mr. Chairman, before leaving the little discussion which we had a few moments ago, and for the benefit of newspaper editors who are writing editorials across Canada rather regularly, I should just like to say that at no time have I ever said, and at no time have I ever been reported as having said, as far as I have seen the press, that oleomargarine is not a good food. As a matter of fact, so far as I know it is just as good a food, from the point of view of food value, as butter. I want to say that because I have read editorials almost daily in which I am quoted as having said something contrary to that. What I always have said is that we do not allow either oleomargarine or butter into this country. Butter comes into this country only under permit, and is presumed to be excluded from every other country, excepting Australia and New Zealand, under a tariff which makes it impossible for it to get in. It has been fourteen cents a pound up to the first of January, and it is twelve cents a pound now. We allow butter to come in under permit only from New Zealand and Australia. I may say that condition was established when my hon. friends on the other side were the government. Since 1931 we have let butter come into this country only under permit. Therefore both butter and oleomargarine are excluded from Canada excepting under very extreme conditions, when butter is allowed in from Australia and New Zealand.
That must have been good legislation.
Well, it was good enough legislation to have been kept on by all governments for some considerable time.
Congratulations.

But that does not say that New Zealand butter is not just as good as Canadian butter, or that Australian butter is not just as good as Canadian butter, and it does not say that oleomargarine is not just as good as any of them. What I am saying is that we do not allow either butter or oleomargarine into this country to compete with our butter. These are facts which one does not need to explain any further.

On a point of order, because I am so often called to order myself, may I ask the minister what his remarks have to do with the item under discussion?

It has exactly just as much to do with it as my hon. friend's question of a few moments ago.
The answer to the question asked a few moments ago in regard to the experimental station in the vicinity of Morden is to this effect, that we have been making soil surveys in order to locate the type of soil which is thought to be necessary to carry out the experiments that we desire to make. It is thought that we have located a suitable place for an experimental station, and when it is established it will be for the purpose of experiments in connection with cereals and forage crops.

I should like to ask a question in that connection. In the riding I happen to have the privilege of representing we produce 85 per cent of the small fruits produced in British Columbia, and British Columbia produces approximately 50 per cent of the small fruits produced in Canada. I refer to raspberries and strawberries. We have had an application in for some time for a small experimental station in the central part of the Fraser valley, which would concern itself particularly with diseases affecting raspberries and strawberries. What steps are contemplated or will be taken in that connection? We have an experimental farm in the riding, but it is primarily interested in dairying and stock production. It has very little connection with small fruits. The soil is not similar to that where most of the small fruits are produced. We have asked for an experimental or illustration station in the central part of the valley-we are not particular where-where 50 per cent of the small fruits of Canada are produced. What steps are being taken in that connection?

I understand that at Mission there is a station operating in connection with berries. Then, there is, of course, the Agassiz farm. The work at Mission is being carried on under the direction of the officials from the Agassiz farm; but if I interpret the hon. member's question correctly he has an idea that there should be another station established somewhere in the vicinity of the area where the airport is.

Somewhere near
where the berries are produced.

Some consideration has been given to that. I am not in a position
to make any definite statement as to what will be done there, but consideration is being given to the matter.

I want to make it clear that I am not in a critical mood on this matter, but the experimental station or the illustration station, I believe they call it, is at Hatzic. It is on a private individual's farm, where apparently, through the Department of Agriculture, we make certain arrangements for the production of small fruits. This is a very large industry. For instance, last year one co-operative alone shipped $1,500,000 worth of small fruits to Britain. It is no small industry which can ship $1,500,000 worth of raspberries and strawberries to Britain alone.
What we are asking for is an illustration station, or if you prefer to call it an experimental farm or station, somewhere in the central part of the valley. We particularly want it in the area where the berries are grown, because if you are to control the diseases, and find out the different varieties of berries that we can produce, the station should obviously be where the soil is capable of producing the maximum crops. We are not asking for a large experimental farm; we are asking for an experimental station. The potato growers of British Columbia asked for the same thing. We in the upper part of the valley are quite agreeable that that station should be placed in the riding of the hon. member for New Westminster, because that is where most of the potatoes of the province of British Columbia are grown. At least, they are grown in the lower part of the province.
We are having a great deal of difficulty with disease, particularly among our raspberries. We realize now that because the British markets ate cut off we must either cut our cost of production or increase our production under nominal costs or find other markets for other varieties. One way that could be brought about is by establishing what we call an illustration station somewhere in the vicinity of where the maximum production takes place. I would strongly urge upon the minister that consideration be given to establishing one. It would entail very small cost because, as I said before, one co-operative alone shipped $1,500,000 worth of small fruits to Great Britain. That is no small amount, and it is only part of our production.

I might answer this question before we go on to something else. I was in Vancouver the day before yesterday, and the berry growers, to whom reference has been made, interviewed me there with regard to this matter and other matters having to do with the marketing of their berry crops. All I can
Supply-Agriculture

say to the hon. member is that we realize that there is a necessity for carrying on experimental work there on a larger scale than we are now carrying it on. Consideration will be given to the representations which he has made.

It is my understanding that two experimental stations were to be established in Alberta to operate in conjunction with the Lacombe experimental farm. I also understand that these stations were to give special consideration to the study of the wooded grey soils found in the foothill territories of Alberta. Have these two stations been established? If so, where?

I understand that there are stations established between Lacombe and the mountain area. I am not able to give the exact location of them. At these two stations they are proceeding to make a study of the soils.

Under this item I should like to ask the minister whether the experimental fur farm at Summerside comes under this vote, or under some other? If it does, I should like to have some information with regard to the progress of that farm and the amount of stock there.
It does come under this vote, yes.
May I have some information with regard to the cost of this farm? What is it doing? There is no report on it.
The work is educational, carried on in connection with nutrition and genetics in different types of foxes.

In view of the observations of the hon. member for Fraser Valley about being in order, I think I shall be in order in asking the minister whether any thought has been given to establishing an experimental farm or illustration station to study the development of oil crops in this country, having regard to the great public interest in certain phases of that matter. Having got into order, I wish to thank him for the clear statement he made on the butter and margarine situation, in which he said that margarine was by no means an inferior food, and he gave reasons why he was opposed to the introduction of foreign butter or margarine. I see he is much in favour of the manufacture of butter within the country, so that I am sure the committee would be interested to know what his attitude is to the manufacture of margarine in Canada.
I do not think this is the item under which that should be considered. The desire is to have this item stand, and go on.

It has been suggested to me that it would be of benefit to some of the tobacco growers if a short course were given in the grading of tobacco. It is an intricate process. There are thirty odd grades and subgrades of tobacco, and, when buyers go into the field to buy, some of the farmers and growers are more or less at a disadvantage because they are not thoroughly familiar with the different grades. As I say, it has been suggested that a short course of a week or two would be beneficial. Has the department had any suggestions of that kind, or would it be possible for the substation at Delhi to carry out that work?

I understand that there is an arrangement between the companies concerned and the government whereby the department gives assistance to schools which are conducted by the companies, and assistance is also given by the companies. At any rate they have representation in similar schools in connection with production, these being conducted by governmental authorities. In other words, there is a co-operative arrangement to assist graders of tobacco, but I presume what the hon. member advocates is a government school apart from those.

I was not suggesting that instruction be given to the graders, but that the growers themselves should be instructed so that they may be familiar with their own grades of tobacco when the company graders come.

I understand that the province puts on short courses which the producers attend, but we have no part in those.
I suppose that would be extension work from Guelph college.
I did not know there was any.

Arising out of the answer given to the hon. member for Fraser Valley, I should like to know whether the illustration station spoken of as likely to be established in the Fraser valley will be expected to deal with the whole province of British Columbia. Will it take care of the needs of the Okanagan valley and the Creston valley area, for instance?

We have twenty illustration stations in British Columbia, and in the Okanagan we have the Summerland farm, which is perhaps the most advanced experi-

Supply-Agriculture
mental farm we have in Canada dealing with fruits. The station I speak of would be only one out of twenty-one if it were established as another station. We have twenty others spread over the province.

Does the department
make grants to illustration stations owned by private farmers? There are several in my constituency and it has become difficult for these individual farmers to keep up these orchards or illustration stations. If they were given some assistance I think these stations would serve a useful and beneficial purpose in the communities concerned.

We have a great many stations of the type referred to where we go on to the farms of fairly successful farmers or men who do not raise objection to people going on their land, being themselves prepared to explain the experiments to those interested. We rent from fifteen acres of land up from these men, and for a small rental they agree to take instruction from our officials as to how to proceed with the plots and with the work done there. They also agree to allow the public to go on the land and see the experimental work which is being done, and in return for that they have the right to sell the crop when it matures and dispose of it for their own good. That is carried on across Canada and there are many of these farms in western Canada.
No direct grants are given?
A rental is given; that is all.

I think I should say a word with reference to our experimental farm station about twelve miles southwest of Fort William. If all the work the government does, and the money it spends, bring as good results as those obtained on that station, there is no doubt about the future of the government's policy. The experiments in grains and grasses, fruits and vegetables of different types, fertilizer, and all the diseases that attack fruits and vegetables, are excellent. As the minister has said, people are allowed to go on t'he farm, and there is a big field day. The experiment superintendent is a man who knows his work, and with it he is most courteous and kind.
Item agreed to.

speechtext:
Item 15 stands. Production service-
16. Production service administration, $46,089.

I wish to refer to a matter which perhaps does not come directly under this vote, though it might as well. I refer to
the bulletins put out by the department. They are fine bulletins and I know they are in great demand, but in the past several months I have found that many of them are out of print, owing, I presume, to that demand. Is any provision made for augmenting the supply or increasing the production for the coming months? I feel that it is a service which should be extended.
They are being replenished just as quickly as that can be done. We agree there is some lack of them at the moment, but we are attempting to bring them up to date.

Item agreed to.
Production service-Health of animals-
17. Administration of Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and Meat and Canned Foods Act, $2,611,508.

There is an increase of
8238,909 in this item, and I see it is mainly. accounted for by salaries. I think the county of Huron is fourth in line for a tested area. If this increase does not mean we are to get any more service than we have had in the past, our people will be disappointed. I do not object to these men getting better salaries, but certainly we need better service. Could the minister tell us whether this increase will mean better service, or if it is just an increase in salaries?

As has been indicated, this increase is largely accounted for by salaries, which will not mean additional staff; but a considerable portion will go to increased staff, and to the extent that this is so, the service will be increased. This year we are taking third year students at the veterinary college at Guelph and sending them out to do much of the work that has to be done under this item. Of course that will involve not only a good deal in the way of payments but also a good deal in the way of expenses.
Will that by any chance speed up the service that we were to get in connection with tested areas?
Yes, that is exactly why it is being done. The idea is to speed up the inspection work being done in connection with T.B. and other work of that kind.
If that is the case could the minister give us any idea when our area will be tested? I think we are fourth in line.
We are hoping to get at it this year.

A farmer in my district has a purebred Hereford herd, and he has lost three of his cattle. Sometimes they break
Supply-Agriculture

out in a sweat; they gradually get thinner and thinner until they die. Would the minister have any idea what the disease might be?

I do not think it would be possible even to make a guess. The proper thing, of course, would be to get the nearest veterinary, either one of our men or someone else, to examine these cattle. I should think it important that they are examined.

Last fall they very kindly sent two men from Ottawa, but they could not tell what the disease was. More recently I have been after them to send another man, but they advised me to get in touch with the experimental farm at Guelph. We have had men from there, too.

Could the minister indicate whether any action is being taken with a view to training a larger number of veterinary 'surgeons? I understand that there is quite a shortage all across Canada, that not enough are graduating to fill the government service. I believe the governments of Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan-and Manitoba, too, I am informed-are making special grants to students, and I believe the federal government should participate in some such program to train veterinary surgeons, so that it may be possible to meet the problems which are being brought to the department.

Some 130 will graduate next year. I believe there were about thirty-eight last year; there will be about forty this year, and about 130 or 140 next year. That will give some idea of the increased numbers. Probably that is partly due to the fact that quite a number of men who came back from overseas went to the veterinary college at Guelph and are being trained for that work.
During an earlier stage of the discussion- I have forgotten what we were considering at the time-I made the statement that we were 120 short in our own staff, and I want to get that on Hansard correctly now. When I read my remarks on the previous occasion I found that the 120 had become one or two; probably that has something to do with shorthand, but the statement should have been that we were 120 short in our own staff. And of course there is a great shortage throughout the country, so that we are encouraging these men to go into that work. One way of giving encouragement is to employ them as third-year students to go out and do work. This year we are sending out 114 students from Guelph and another group of about fifteen from Quebec. That is being done to give these men assistance during the summer so that they may continue

their college courses in the winter, and at the same time gain a great deal of experience in the work they will be required to do later on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Last year when this item was before the committee I brought to the attention of the minister the difficulty under which farmers in my constituency are operating because of the lack of veterinarians and the T.B. testing. At that time the minister was good enough to tell me the situation and that he would take my representations into careful consideration. Is he now in a position to say what progress has been made and what we may look forward to in the matter of help in the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg?

It does not appear that we shall have enough men to get down to that area this year, certainly not in the early part of the season. The position which has developed since the matter was brought up last year is I think, pretty well illustrated by the figures I have given and by our undertaking to students to put them in the field in their third year. That is an encouragement, of course, to some who would find it difficult to get through without that work. It also increases the staffs we have available to carry on the work. The 130 or so who are going out this year will be of great help in strengthening the staffs we have out through the country and making it possible for us to get the work done much more quickly. I am sorry we shall not have sufficient'to get down to the hon. member's constituency this year, but we shall be there just as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Could the minister indicate approximately when he might expect his men to reach that constituency?
Next year for sure, I am told.

I am interested in this item
because we have had an outbreak of virulent T.B. in my constituency. On this item I have usually spoken of Bang's Disease, or contagious abortion, and that problem still exists. But in the district surrounding my home we have something really worse. One of the finest herds in the district has gone down completely on a T.B. test; and it was an accredited herd. Within the year that herd has been negative. It has always been negative; it has never had any trouble with T.B. This year on a test the whole herd went down, including even this year's calves. Several other herds in the neighbourhood have gone down in the same way. Apparently the infection, whatever it is or wherever it is coming from, is of a most virulent type. Although admittedly men have

Supply-Agriculture
been up there and have furnished every assistance they could, apparently they are at a loss to find the cause of the infection.
So far as the manager of the herd is concerned, let me say that the man who owns the herd, and his son, are men who are well trained in the raising of purebred stock. As I said, this is one of the finest herds in the country, a herd which has been responsible for the producing of a Canadian champion.
I went out to see this herd, and what I saw was really pitiful. The owner led me around and said "There is the reserve champion of last year's winter fair." He showed me some heifers. They have not been able to find the cause of infection, and they are doing testing there now.
I was present the other morning when the report on another fine purebred herd was read, and ten purebred cows had gone down. I do not think any ruling has yet been made as to the cause of infection. Let us consider the condition of the first purebred herd. This man's young cattle were sent away to pasture 'last year on the day they were tested. They were negative at that time. They were brought in early in November, and every one of those had gone down in this year's test.
This would seem to me to be an unusual case, and there must be an unusual cause for the infection in that area. I have tried to find the cause of infection, and I am led to believe that it has occurred either through an interchange of feed bags-and that is a common procedure at the present time on these farms-or it has occurred by the feeding of bone meal. There does not seem to be any other reason for it.
This year's calves by this purebred herd went down. It might be that the cause of infection of the calves was due to feeding, but they have been fed pasteurized skim milk. This is a serious question, because not only am I interested in the matter since it affects these purebred herds in my district which are going down, but I am interested as a physician in the cause of a contagious disease. I say that because bovine tuberculosis is so readily transferable to human beings, particularly to children. In children it cripples, incapacitates and destroys. I would say that a fair percentage of tuberculosis in children is due to bovine tuberculosis.
The other day, Friday last, the Prime Minister brought in a resolution telling what the government intended to do by way of grants for the cure of tuberculosis. But if we are not going to start on this thing at the bottom, and if this is not going to be cleared up, there is no use in talking about the 5849-272
eradication of tuberculosis in human beings. We know the pitiful effects on children who catch the disease, and the crippled joints from which they suffer.
In that district we have a very fine agricultural representative. He has been giving every encouragement to young farmers there by way of calf clubs, and all that sort of thing. I have tried to take interest in these matters. But it is hard to tell those young fellows to raise good stock or to go into the raising of purebred stock when they know that they may be wiped out at any time on account of a disease like this.
I am appealing to the minister for additional help by way of men in that area, so that we may have more than the ordinary T.B. test. In the ordinary T.B. test a few animals in a herd may go down here and there, throughout the area. But this is wiping out herds. We are proud of some of our herds there. These men who have other good herds coming up for tests simply feel that they are sitting on a bomb, knowing that the work of a lifetime may be wiped out.
I am still of the opinion that this is no ordinary disease, because it possesses a virulence which has not been exhibited in any T.B. area before, and I say the department should do experimental work to find the cause of that trouble.
As I said earlier, I believe the matter of feeding bone meal to these animals has had a great deal to do with it, either that or the exchange of feed bags. Above all, I would say to the minister that the farmers should be given an educational program as to how the disease could be avoided. I met the veterinary for that area at one of these herds the other morning, and we were absolutely at a loss to know what the cause of the infection could be.

The case referred to is a special one. As the hon. member has said, our men have been checking up and doing the best they can to determine the cause. As a matter of fact, we have taken such particular care with it that the director, himself, has been out there and has gone over those herds. Not only that, but he has personally checked the work done by those who have been attempting to determine whether it is ordinary bovine tuberculosis. He is satisfied that it is. It may be a particularly virulent type, but they are satisfied that that is what it is.
Then, as for being able to establish definitely where it has originated* let me say they have not been successful in that up to
Supply-Agriculture

the present time. However, it is being treated as a very special case, and the men are right on the work of trying to determine the cause ond how to overcome similar happenings in that area or elsewhere. Beyond that, however, they have not been able to go, up to the present time.

The department has furnished every aid and facility, so far as that is concerned. But I should like to ask the minister if they have considered the possibility of its having originated in this interchange of feed bags, or if they have made investigation into the bone meal products these farmers are feeding?

They have fairly well satisfied themselves that the disease has not been brought in either through the bone meal or the sacks. As a matter of fact they are inclined to believe it has been brought in by animals which have been brought in from areas which are not inspected. Up to the present time they have not been able to prove that definitely, but that is their opinion.

In the first herd which went down, one of the finest in the country, there has been no interchange of cattle, so far as that is concerned. And even this year's calves have gone down. We investigated the other morning the possibility of the disease being conveyed to them by skim milk; but the farmers have been feeding pasteurized milk. They have had no new stock in there. This man breeds his own, and has not been buying any; unless the disease was taken in there by drovers; and it would hardly seem possible that a drover using a truck could bring in a disease of that virulence.

There is nothing more I can add to what I have said, other than this, that it would not be necessary for the animal to come into the herd that suffered most in the end. It may have come into the district by that method. Then again, these animals have been exhibited over a large area, and it is possible that some of them could have picked up the disease and passed it on to the others.
I may say I had some experience with a herd of cattle, myself, at the end of the first war. I had seventeen in that herd, and sixteen out of the seventeen went down. We just had to get rid of them; that is all. I started with the one that was left, and I have not had one go down since. The one left was a calf. One cannot explain how it happens sometimes. I am quite convinced, so far as my case was concerned, that it happened through a cow I had had on the farm for a long time. She began to get thin, but I did

not have her checked immediately. I had no particular reason for doing it at that time. However, by the time I got around to checking them, every animal in the herd, with the exception of the one calf, went down. These things can happen anywhere if one is not careful, and I have no doubt that something like that happened to that herd.

The four other herds which went down had not been exhibited at the winter fair and there did not seem to be any contact between the herds. That is why I feel so disturbed that a disease of such virulence has come into the area.
We are doing everything we can about it.
Is the T.B. test compulsory anywhere in Canada?

Areas take a vote by counties or municipalities and when there are two-thirds in favour of it, then it is compulsory. Everyone must have his animals checked. As a matter of fact we check and inspect the animals in the whole district. No one is allowed to bring animals into the district until they are inspected, and persons who have animals in the district are not allowed to have those animals come into contact with others if it can be avoided.

I do not think that is good enough. I have had some experience with bovine tuberculosis and, like the hon. member for Lanark, I think we have to go further and have the testing compulsory right across Canada. I think it is wrong to leave it to a vote whether there will be inspection and testing. We had a case in our district and the first we knew of it was when a little baby took sick. We had a hard job getting the baby to the hospital, but I am not going to tell that story.
The baby died and the medical man who had attended the baby diagnosed the case as bovine tuberculosis. He immediately had a veterinary sent out to the farm and the cow that was milking reacted. When we killed the cow she was absolutely rotten. I would have thought that after that had happened everyone in the district would have been conscious of the danger and been willing to have his herd tested, but even the man who had been supplying the milk to the village refused to have his herd tested.
This matter is so dangerous that we should have a law to compel every farmer to have every animal tested periodically. A man may have his herd tested and found to be free but, like the herd the hon. member for Lanark

Supply-Agriculture
spoke of, there may be another herd on the adjoining farm or a little way off. The cattle happen to get in contact with each other or a truck comes in that has been hauling other cattle. There is always the danger of losing the whole herd. In addition, as the hon. member for Lanark said, there is a danger to human beings, especially to children who are so susceptible to this disease. The minister should consider bringing in a measure covering the whole of Canada and making testing compulsory.

I should like to put on the record what has been done. The following are the percentages of cattle that have been tested:

Nova Scotia	 02
New Brunswick	 100
Quebec	 00
Ontario	 00
Manitoba	 50
Saskatchewan	 40
Alberta	 12

That does not say that any particular area has had everything done for it that it desires to have done. The testing of entire areas was taken on much more readily in the maritime provinces than anywhere else. It is only since I came into the department that Alberta has permitted us to go into the province and check the cattle. You will notice that only twelve per cent of the cattle in Alberta have been covered. That is due to the fact that we have not had sufficient men since that time to do this work. During the thirties, as everyone knows, veterinaries throughout the country were almost starved out of practice because animals were not worth enough to warrant calling a veterinary when they were sick. Many of these men went out of practice and there has been great difficulty of late in finding enough men to cover the areas.
There is no difficulty in getting the money. This is one item in my estimates in connection with which I can get all the money that can be spent each year, provided that. I can get the men to spend it and do the work. We are trying to build up staffs by encouraging men to come in and qualify to do this work. Until a year ago we were probably a little overzealous in insisting that any man who did this work must be specially qualified. We were hesitant about putting anyone on the work who had not passed a special examination. It was not enough that he had been a veterinary thirty years or twenty-five years ago; he had to pass an examination now.
Since about two years ago we have been trying to utilize every available man and we
5849-272i
have even had students out doing the work.
I do not think we are in position where we could compel people to have their herds tested because we could not test them. There are not enough veterinaries in the country to test them. As is indicated here, there are some sections of the country that have been at this a long time and have had the work done. However, the fact that they have been tested once does not indicate that during all the years they have kept right up to date. The only reason they have not been kept up to date is that we have not enough men.

I am glad to hear the minister say that they are not being so fussy about veterinaries during the past year or two. Would it be possible to organize teams of men who were not veterinaries to work under a veterinary? I have seen cattle tested, and it does not seem to me that it is necessary to have a veterinary do the actual injecting of the virus and make the examination. If a group of men were trained to work with a veterinary I think they could cover the country a lot faster.

I just want to follow up what the hon. member for The Battlefords has said. In the particular district in which I live we have a T.B. free area. You must get a permit to bring in cattle; you must have them tested and all that. As nearly as I can remember, it is twelve years since those municipalities were brought into the T.B. free area and there has not been a re-check since that time. All young stock that have been born have not been checked and there has been no check on whether an animal with a contagious disease is among the herds.
I could cite many cases, such as the one cited by the hon. member for The Battlefords, that occurred when we had the first test. Many families with little children were very much alarmed and in some cases entire herds went down. It seems to me that something must be done. Twelve years is too long a period to let pass without a check. I realize all the difficulties the minister has pointed out. I remember advocating that he organize students in teams under qualified veterinaries. If that will not accomplish the work, then you might have to go further and follow the suggestion of the hon. member for The Battlefords.
This is a serious business because it affects human life. I hope the department will give serious consideration to the development of teams to work under properly qualified veterinaries, not only to take care of new areas but to check the old areas. I know of areas that have applied to become free areas, but they have not been able to be declared free areas because of

Supply-Agriculture
a shortage of help. Certainly these areas which have not been inspected for ten or twelve years should be re-checked, because you cannot tell what may have developed in that time. I want to impress the importance of this on the minister.

I was delighted to hear the minister say that they are going to employ extra veterinary surgeons for this work. 1 was also pleased to hear him say that he has no trouble in getting the money to do the job. I am very much interested in the question of re-testing raised by the hon. member for Souris. I happen to live in a T.B. free area. It is not so long ago as twelve years that we had our re-test, because they are always picking out the odd animal that will go down. I have been very much interested in this matter for a number of years, and I quite appreciate the alarm felt by the hon. member for Lanark and the hon. member for The Battlefords, because since I came to this House of Commons I have seen T.B. tested cows go into an area where there were people suffering from T.B. and six months later when the cattle were tested they also were found to have T.B. That is a serious matter. I am delighted that the department is carrying on this work.
* There is another point I would bring to the minister's attention. When he became Minister of Agriculture more areas were coming in than are coming in now. The movement started in the eastern provinces and everybody was more agreeable then to coming in because cattle then were worth S40 to $45 apiece. The same grade of cow brings $200 today. When you go into a municipality and want to sign up the farmers to have this testing done, naturally they say: Well, cattle are a good price today. If the man has a family of small children he may look at the matter differently, but if he looks at it only from the point of view of dollars and cents he says: Thirty-eight dollars does not look very much to me for a cow that will go into the tank; I will leave it until later on. Naturally, under those circumstances, you do not get two-thirds of your people to agree to have the test. I spoke about this matter in the house once before and one hon. member pointed out that you got $96. It is true that you got $96 if your animal was registered and you had papers and all that sort of thing, but I have always been in the class, when milking cows for the city of Winnipeg, of being glad to get a good grade cow.
A registered cow is worth several hundred dollars now.

I never had money enough to buy anything like that. I want to appeal to

the minister to check up with his officials, because I think $38 compensation is far too little to pay, with the price of cattle what it is today. I assure the minister that I am hopeful that, as long as he is Minister of Agriculture, he will never let prices go back to $40 and $50 for a cow as long as we have the United States market willing to pay a good price for our cows. I think $38 is ridiculous. If you doubled that figure and then went out and asked farmers to sign up I am sure they would agree to have the test made in much greater numbers than they are doing now. In the interests of health alone it should be made compulsory. I am naturally afraid, in this house, of talking about compulsion, because I know what would be said of me if I did. Nevertheless, in the interests of the health of this nation, I do say that this testing should be made compulsory.

I just want to say in reply that our experience is in the opposite direction. We have seventy districts in Saskatchewan which have already applied and to which we have not been able to send anybody, and we also have a considerable number waiting in Ontario. If we were anywhere near up to date we would probably have double the present number applying right away.
I am delighted to hear that.

There is no difficulty in getting applications. They are coming in so fast that we are not able to handle them.
The other question is one which has been discussed in the house several times; that is, about compensation going up and down with the price of cattle. There are arguments in favour of that and against it. When cattle were down, for example, to $50 apiece, and sometimes as low as $20 apiece, the argument then was that we Should pay more because of the low price of cattle. I think the argument for that was just as strong as the argument that we should pay more when the animal is worth more. There is an argument both ways, but we found it was wise up to the present to maintain the same level whether prices are high or low.

You do not get anything if your animal goes into the tank. If your animal is only partly diseased, around the neck, say, or the liver, you get what value is in the meat, but you do not get anything if it goes into the tank.
You get whatever value there is in the hide and grease. It may not be much, but you get it.

That is nothing.

At present it may
amount to quite a bit.

On previous occasions I have warned the minister and the department of the seriousness of T.B. and also Bang's disease in cattle, and I want to take this opportunity to reiterate in part what I have said before. I think it all hinges around one thing. I was glad to hear the minister say that he has never been refused any money by the government for this purpose. I think that is all the more reason for stating that the root of the trouble is the low salaries paid to the veterinary surgeons doing this work. I have said that before, and I shall continue to say it until their salaries are in line with those paid to other professions in the department and in the government service. Their salaries are nowhere near in line at present.
I have here a resolution passed at the annual meeting of the Ontario veterinary association, held at Niagara Falls, Ontario, on January 22-23, 1948. It reads:
Copy of resolution unanimously passed at the annual meeting of the Ontario veterinary association held at Niagara Falls, Ontario, on January 22, and 23, 1948.
The Ontario veterinary association now in annual conference at the hotel General Brock, Niagara Falls, Ontario, unanimously endorse the following resolution and respectfully request your sympathetic consideration and action.
Resolved that the salary schedule of veterinarians employed in the federal Department of Agriculture is inadequate for the responsibilities involved and the qualifications required,
The depleted federal service can be restored only by the institution of appropriate and fair salary schedules and will have its reflection on the health status of the Canadian livestock industry as it relates not only to our domestic but export trade.
May we ask your favourable consideration to an upward revision of salaries comparable to that offered members of other professions.
Ontario Veterinary Association,
E. F. Johnston,
President.
What was the date of that?

It was a resolution passed at their convention on January 22 and 23 of this year. I tvant to be quite fair with the department. Some considerable changes have been made and I congratulate the minister upon them. Apparently these changes have not been sufficient to bring recent graduates, or graduates of previous years, into the service of the department. I want to say a few things to prove that statement. As the minister said earlier this evening, the usual personnel of the health of animals branch is 410. The present staff numbers approximately 290. I may be out one or two; but, as the minister said
previously, they are 120 short of the required number to bring it up to the average. In addition to that, sixty members of the present staff are over sixty years of age.
It has already been said that a large number of areas have asked for this test to be taken.
I have some figures here which are probably about a month and a half old. They may not be quite accurate, but they are approximately correct. I should like to put them on the record. Areas which have been accredited but are now past due on their tests total ninety-six. Areas that are in the process of being tested across Canada-that is, about a month ago-number twenty-seven. Areas accepted for this test but not tested at all number fourteen. Areas due for a test during 1948 number thirty. That makes a total of 126 areas across Canada waiting for the T.B. test. Unless something is done to encourage graduate veterinarians, or graduates of previous years, to come into the service, we shall never get very far ahead with this testing work.
I want to take exception to a statement made by the minister on April 17. I do not know whether it was a mistake of the press or not; I should not like to say, but the minister can correct me if I am wrong. In a statement made by the minister to the Kiwanis club in Ottawa on April 17 of this year, the following appears. I shall quote just part of it:
Mr. Gardiner stressed the need for more "properly qualified veterinarians" in Canada. In Canada there were 904 properly qualified vets and 294 of them worked for the government. Fifty-five of the government employees were more than sixty years of age. At the present time there were 120 vacancies in the Department of Agriculture for vets.
That does not agree with the figures I have of the number of registered veterinarians across Canada. I have the figures for the various provinces, but it is not necessary to give them. The total across Canada as I have them-I may be out a few-is 1,053. I think there are somewhere between that number and 1,100 in Canada.
I want to congratulate the department and the veterinary college of Guelph for getting together and co-operating on taking the third-year students. Part of the third-year course at the veterinary college is to take on this work for two months in the summer. Therefore the third year will be the fourth year now, since the veterinary course will be a five-year course from now on. I may say that the number graduating this year from the veterinary college at Guelph is forty-three. The 1949 class, that is, the boys who will be taken on by the department this year for the
Supply-Agriculture

two-month period, one month in field work on the disease of plants and plant inspection, is 118. The number in the class which will graduate in 1950 is 140, and the number in the class of 1951 is 153. It will be seen by these figures that there will be an increasing number in those years. I should like the minister to answer at a later time, if he can, just how many of this year's students, the forty-three graduating this year, he expects to take on the department this year. I doubt whether there will be very many.
Several orders in council have been passed respecting the salaries of veterinary surgeons. As I said before, some increases have been given. Some of these orders in council have been tabled in the last few days, but until that time they had not been tabled. I wonder why this government passes orders in council and makes them available to everybody but members of parliament. I make that statement and it is true, because I had a difficult time to get the three last orders in council. I knew they had been passed. I had a terrific time in getting hold of them. They had never been tabled, but everybody but members of parliament seemed to be able to get hold of them. I ask the minister why that is, because surely we have the same privileges as an individual in having access to orders in council passed by the government.
An order in council was passed on March 24, P.C. 1/1222, which increased the starting salary of veterinarians from $2,100 to $2,400; but the $2,100 starting salary is still retained in the order in council. If in future years they wish to drop back to $2,100, because there are probably a few more vets in the country, they can drop back to that amount. As I said, the starting salary was raised on March 24 to $2,400, and on a later date it was raised to $2,700. So far as I know, that is the starting salary for veterinarians coming into the service under the grade one classification.
Other orders in council have been passed to increase and reclassify veterinarians, now in the service, for which I wish to congratulate the minister, or whoever was responsible for it. That was done more or less to hold the men who are in the service at the present time. It was very necessary to hold these men, because in the past few years we have had 120 resignations, and if something were not done, there probably would have been more resignations from the branch. But, as I said before, nothing very satisfactory has yet been done. I understand that something is now being considered. Since I have heard nothing definite, I shall be glad if the minister can make it definite tonight that the starting salary

has been increased and that the reclassifications can be made to a greater maximum without examination, just simply a year by year reclassification up to a maximum for the grade four veterinarians, or senior veterinarians.
As was so well said by the hon. member for Lanark, this is not a problem of the health of livestock only; it is a national health problem, and should be treated as such. If what we have to do is to pay more to veterinarians to join the service, then it should be done, because we have been going along for three or four years with a reduced staff. It is of sufficient importance not to be so miserly in the future. It is essential that we do something to rid this country of T.B. I repeat that this is not simply a livestock health problem; it is a national health problem. When you find young children coming down with T.B., and the incidence so great as was stated by the hon. member for Lanark, it should make people jealous of the fact that they want to have their herds tested even from that point of view alone.
I would suggest strongly that the department be given sufficient money to carry on a vigorous advertising campaign to warn farmers of the many dangers confronting them in this fight against T.B. It might be logical for a person, after having an accredited herd for sixteen or eighteen years, possibly to become a little careless. That is understandable. He thinks, having been free so long, that condition will continue without as much care on his part as he has taken in the past. These veterinary surgeons should warn these men of the various dangers, and the department should carry on an instructional campaign, telling the farmers of the various things they must guard against.
As the minister has said, the department does not feel that the exchange of feed bags was so very important a factor in the recent outbreak in Lanark county, nor was the bone meal. They think it was introduced by animals from non-tested areas. That is another point that suggests the importance of getting over all areas in the country and not simply choosing isolated counties here and there. A test is of questionable value, when there is a county that is tested regularly while the county next to it is not. A man across the fence might have cattle on his farm; there might be a stream running from his field into the adjoining pasture, and if his cattle were polluted with tuberculosis, his herd not. having been tested, his neighbour's cattle would become infected.

It is important to have the larger areas covered, and more consideration should be given to areas adjoining tuberculosis-tested areas. Consideration should be given them above isolated areas, no matter when the application came in, because it is of much greater importance to have adjoining areas tested than it is to have an isolated area tested.
As the hon. member for Lanark pointed out-, the savings of a lifetime might be wiped out overnight by this dread scourge of tuberculosis. The two diseases that call most urgently for attention are tuberculosis and Bang's disease. On various occasions I have mentioned Bang's and it is equally important with tuberculosis. The area-testing for tuberculosis is, however, of great importance, and Bang's will go along with that.
I wish to congratulate those who have taken part in creating the greater co-operation between the veterinary surgeons and the medical profession, because neither the medical men nor the veterinarians independently could possibly handle the situation. There must be complete co-operation. They must travel hand in hand across the country in the fight to get rid of tuberculosis and Bang's disease. I have made various statements before on this question, and I should like to have the minister inform the committee of the number of veterinarians graduating this year. How many is it expected to obtain from the college?

I am not in a position to say how many we shall get from the college, probably not more than four or five as far as we know at the moment.
I think I should say something with regard to the salary levels. I would agree with the hon. member for Brant that until recently the salaries have been much too low. The ranges ran from SI,640. As a matter of fact, veterinarians came on at SI,640 and worked up to the level of Sl,800-$2,160, and there was some difficulty in getting beyond that level. The situation is changed today, so that the veterinarian, if he is right out of college, comes on at $2,700. He does not come on at the bottom of that grade, which is $2,400 to $2,700, but at the top of the classification, which is $2,700, and he has to put in only one year to get into the $3,000 class. If he has had one year's experience as a veterinarian outside the department he goes into the $3,000 class, and he gets a yearly advancement until he reaches $3,300, without further examination. From $3,300, however, the increases are promotional and he can go up to $4,800. So that
there has been a considerable increase in the payments now made to veterinarians.
Can he go to $4,800 without examination?
He has to have the usual promotional examination from one classification to another after he gets up to $3,300. It is neither an oral nor a written examination but a rating.
That is departmental?

Yes. It is based on the work he has done. It is a departmental rating confirmed by the commission. That is the position in the matter of salaries. I might say, in answer to the question my hon. friend has asked, that the 904 is the figure given at the Chateau Laurier. That is the official figure of registered veterinarians. In addition to that, there are veterinarians who are qualified, working for the department, and that would bring the figure to between 1,100 and 1,200.
I understood the minister to say the figure he gave included 294 working for the department.
The 904 is exclusive rather than inclusive.

The minister said that the veterinarians could go to $4,800 without examination. That is perfectly true. They can probably do so if they get a reclassification in their grades and are good enough to be chief veterinary inspector, meat inspection, or chief veterinary inspector, animal contagious diseases. There are only two jobs and only two men on those jobs with $4,800. How many men have a chance to get those jobs?

The district inspector, grade 2, can go on to $4,800 as well. There are five of these.
